knowledge_statements.title: Node–Arc Incidence Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard capacitated minimum-cost flow representation using a directed node–arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, and define \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\) by \(B_{va}=1\) when arc \(a\) enters node \(v\), \(B_{va}=-1\) when it leaves \(v\), and \(B_{va}=0\) otherwise. Given costs \(c\in\mathbb R^A\), balances \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), and bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^A\) with \(\ell\le u\), the node–arc model is \[\min\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}.\] Feasibility requires \(\mathbf 1^\top b=0\) on every weakly connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc variables obey node balances through the incidence matrix and independent lower and upper bounds; total prescribed balance must vanish on each component.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
\(\ell\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is the node–arc incidence representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncapacitated minimum-cost network-flow formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents balanced minimum-cost flow as a node–arc LP, records the source's dummy-demand construction for positive aggregate surplus, and distinguishes the capacitated variant. The extract does not state a balancing construction for negative aggregate surplus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. Associate with each node \(i\in V\) an imbalance \(b_i\), where \(b_i>0\), \(b_i<0\), and \(b_i=0\) denote supply, demand, and transshipment nodes, respectively. For each arc \((i,j)\in A\), let \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) be its flow and \(c_{ij}\) its unit cost. If \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\), the uncapacitated minimum-cost flow model is
\[
\min \sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}-\sum_{k:(k,i)\in A}x_{ki}=b_i\quad(i\in V),
\qquad x_{ij}\ge0\quad((i,j)\in A).
\]
If \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i>0\), the source restores aggregate balance by adding a dummy demand node \(d\) with \(b_d=-\sum_{i\in V}b_i\) and zero-cost arcs from every supply node to \(d\). Imposing arc upper bounds gives the capacitated variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced directed network can be represented as a linear program that minimizes total arc cost subject to nonnegative flows and a nodal balance equation requiring net outflow at each node to equal its supply or demand. For positive aggregate surplus, the source adds a dummy demand node with the opposite imbalance and zero-cost arcs from every supply node. The extract gives no corresponding construction for aggregate deficit. Adding arc upper bounds produces the capacitated variant.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is a finite directed graph}
x_{ij}\ge 0\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in A
\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\quad\text{for the balanced formulation}
\text{No arc upper bounds are imposed in the uncapacitated model}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\ \sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}-\sum_{k:(k,i)\in A}x_{ki}=b_i\ \forall i\in V,\ x\ge0\right\},\quad\text{with the stated dummy-demand construction only when }\sum_{i\in V}b_i>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network flows and node conservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative arc flows, conservation at ordinary nodes, source-sink exceptions, and the cycle requirement for a nonzero circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite directed network, every existing arc \((i,j)\) may carry a flow \(x_{ij}\ge 0\). At each node \(i\) that is neither a source nor a sink, conservation requires \(\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}-\sum_{k:(k,i)\in E}x_{ki}=0\). A source may have positive net outflow, and a sink may have positive net inflow. If the network has no sources or sinks and supports a nonzero conserved flow, then it contains a directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each directed arc may carry a nonnegative flow. At an ordinary node, total outgoing flow equals total incoming flow; sources may have positive net outflow and sinks positive net inflow. A network without sources or sinks can support a nonzero conserved flow only if it contains a directed cycle.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite directed network.}
x_{ij}\ge 0\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in E.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i\in V\setminus(S\cup T),\quad \sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}-\sum_{k:(k,i)\in E}x_{ki}=0;\qquad S=T=\varnothing,\ x\not\equiv0\implies G\text{ contains a directed cycle.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacitated network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directed network with nonnegative upper-flow bounds assigned to specified arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A capacitated network is a directed network in which a specified subset \(E_c\subseteq E\) of arcs is assigned nonnegative capacities \(k_{ij}\ge 0\). For every \((i,j)\in E_c\), the capacity is the maximum allowable arc flow, so \(0\le x_{ij}\le k_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated network assigns a nonnegative capacity to specified directed arcs. The nonnegative flow on each such arc cannot exceed its assigned capacity.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a directed network.}
E_c\subseteq E,\qquad k_{ij}\ge 0\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in E_c.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall(i,j)\in E_c,\qquad 0\le x_{ij}\le k_{ij}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite commodity set and \(A\) a finite arc set. For each \(k\in K\), let \(d_k\in\mathbb R_+\) be its demand, let \(\mathcal P_k\) be a finite set of admissible directed paths, and let \(f_p^k\in\mathbb R_+\) be the flow assigned to \(p\in\mathcal P_k\). For \(a\in A\) and \(p\in\mathcal P_k\), let \(\delta_{ap}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether \(p\) uses \(a\). Given capacities \(u_a\in\mathbb R_+\) and arc costs \(c_a^k\in\mathbb R\), the path-flow LP is \[\min\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_k}\left(\sum_{a\in A}c_a^k\delta_{ap}\right)f_p^k\] subject to \[\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_k}f_p^k=d_k\quad(k\in K),\qquad \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_k}\delta_{ap}f_p^k\le u_a\quad(a\in A).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each variable carries one commodity along an admissible path; demand constraints prescribe total path flow, and arc-capacity constraints couple the commodities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite commodity set and \(A\) a finite arc set. For each \(k\in K\), let \(d_k\in\mathbb R_+\) be its demand, let \(\mathcal R_k\) be a finite catalogue of admissible origin-destination routes, and let \(q_r^k\in\mathbb R_+\) be the flow assigned to \(r\in\mathcal R_k\). For \(a\in A\), let \(u_a\in\mathbb R_+\) be its capacity, let \(c_a^k\in\mathbb R\) be its cost for commodity \(k\), and let \(D_{ar}^k\in\mathbb Z_+\) count the traversals of \(a\) by \(r\). The route-flow LP is \[\min\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_k}\left(\sum_{a\in A}c_a^kD_{ar}^k\right)q_r^k\] subject to \[\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_k}q_r^k=d_k\quad(k\in K),\qquad \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_k}D_{ar}^kq_r^k\le u_a\quad(a\in A).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route variables allocate each commodity's demand among a supplied finite catalogue, while route-arc traversal counts determine capacity usage and arc-additive cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(k\in K\), suppose there is a bijection \(\phi_k:\mathcal P_k\to\mathcal R_k\) such that \(D_{a,\phi_k(p)}^k=\delta_{ap}\) for every \(a\in A\) and \(p\in\mathcal P_k\). Then the substitution \(q_{phi_k(p)}^k=f_p^k\) is a linear bijection between the path-flow and route-flow feasible sets. It preserves every demand equality, arc load, and arc-additive objective value. More generally, if \(\mathcal P'_k\subsetneq\mathcal P_k\) and a route catalogue is in incidence-preserving bijection with \(\mathcal P'_k\), then its formulation represents the restriction of the path-flow feasible set to paths in \(\mathcal P'_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence-preserving bijections between paths and routes yield isomorphic LPs; a catalogue corresponding to a proper subset of admissible paths yields the associated restricted formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded, possibly minimum-cost circulation on a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have node–arc incidence matrix \(B\). A circulation is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) satisfying \(Bx=0\). Given arc bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^A\) with \(\ell\le u\), a feasible bounded circulation additionally satisfies \(\ell\le x\le u\). With costs \(c\in\mathbb R^A\), the minimum-cost circulation model is \[\min\{c^\top x:Bx=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\}.\] Thus every node has equal total inflow and outflow, while all remaining restrictions are arc-local.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circulation conserves flow at every node; bounded minimum-cost circulation adds arc bounds and minimizes linear arc cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(\ell\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible exactly when \(Bx=0\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).

children.title: Cycle-Space Flow Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Space Flow Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-algebraic representation of real circulations by a cycle-space basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with incidence matrix \(B\), and let \(C\in\mathbb R^{A\times q}\) have columns forming a basis of \(\ker B\), for example signed fundamental-cycle vectors of a spanning forest. Then \[Bx=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=Cz\text{ for a unique }z\in\mathbb R^q.\] Hence a bounded circulation LP is represented in cycle coordinates by \[\min\{(C^\top c)^\top z:\ell\le Cz\le u\}.\] For a graph with \(\kappa\) weak components, \(q=|A|-|V|+\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle basis parametrizes every real circulation uniquely, converting conservation equations into cycle coordinates while retaining transformed arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: The columns of \(C\) form a basis of \(\ker B\).
\(G\) has \(\kappa\) weakly connected components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker B=\{Cz:z\in\mathbb R^q\}\) with \(q=|A|-|V|+\kappa\).

children.title: Cycle–Circulation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between circulation spaces and cycle-generated flows.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle–Circulation Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic decomposition of nonnegative directed circulations into directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(B\) be its node–arc incidence matrix. If \(x\in\mathbb R_+^A\) satisfies \(Bx=0\), then there exist directed simple cycles \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), coefficients \(\lambda_i>0\), and their zero–one arc-incidence vectors \(\chi^{C_i}\) such that \[x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\chi^{C_i}.\] Conversely, every nonnegative conic combination of directed-cycle incidence vectors satisfies \(Bx=0\). One may choose \(m\le |\{a\in A:x_a>0\}|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative circulations are exactly conic combinations of directed-cycle flows, with no more cycles than positive-flow arcs required.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\chi^{C_i}\) for directed simple cycles, and every such sum is a circulation.

notation.meaning: arc-incidence vector of directed cycle C

children.title: Bounded-Flow Reductions
children.top_down_role: Structural reductions involving lower bounds, upper bounds, or residual capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Flow Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of finite lower arc bounds by a variable shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(Bx=b\) and finite arc bounds \(\ell\le x\le u\). Set \(y=x-\ell\). Then \[Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad By=b-B\ell,\ 0\le y\le u-\ell.\] The correspondence \(x=y+\ell\) is bijective. Moreover, \(c^\top x=c^\top y+c^\top\ell\), so minimizers and objective comparisons are preserved after adding the constant \(c^\top\ell\). Thus every finitely lower-bounded flow model reduces to one with zero lower bounds and adjusted node balances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shifting each arc flow by its lower bound produces zero lower bounds, adjusted balances, unchanged residual capacities, and only a constant objective offset.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a node–arc incidence matrix.
\(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^A\) are finite and \(\ell\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The substitution \(y=x-\ell\) bijectively yields \(By=b-B\ell\) and \(0\le y\le u-\ell\).

children.title: Circulation Reductions
children.top_down_role: Conversions from source-based or balance-based networks to circulation form.

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of balanced transshipment to circulation by one auxiliary node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Bx=b\) be a transshipment system with \(\mathbf1^\top b=0\). Add an auxiliary node \(r\). For each node \(v\) with \(b_v>0\), add an arc \(v\to r\) fixed at flow \(b_v\); for each \(v\) with \(b_v<0\), add an arc \(r\to v\) fixed at flow \(-b_v\). With the incidence convention that entering arcs have sign \(+1\), the augmented flow \((x,z)\) satisfies homogeneous conservation exactly when \(Bx=b\). Deleting the fixed auxiliary arcs recovers \(x\), preserving original costs and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed arcs to one auxiliary node absorb prescribed supplies and demands, turning balanced transshipment into a circulation and permitting exact recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbf1^\top b=0\).
Auxiliary arcs have the stated fixed flows and zero cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Bx=b\) holds exactly when the augmented network flow satisfies homogeneous conservation.

children.title: Transshipment Reductions
children.top_down_role: Conversions involving supplies, demands, and intermediate transshipment nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of circulation feasibility to balanced node supplies by fixing a reference flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the bounded circulation system \(Bx=0\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), choose the reference flow \(x^0=\ell\) and set \(y=x-\ell\). Then \[Bx=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad By=-B\ell,\ 0\le y\le u-\ell.\] Since \(\mathbf1^\top B=0\), the induced balance vector \(-B\ell\) sums to zero on every weak component. Hence bounded circulation feasibility is exactly a zero-lower-bound transshipment feasibility problem; the inverse map is \(x=y+\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting lower bounds converts bounded circulation into a zero-lower-bound transshipment problem whose induced node balances are automatically balanced.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a directed incidence matrix.
\(\ell\le u\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(x\mapsto y=x-\ell\) gives a bijection with \(By=-B\ell\), \(0\le y\le u-\ell\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Bx=b\), where the incidence convention assigns sign \(+1\) to an arc entering a node and \(-1\) to an arc leaving a node, and suppose \(\mathbf 1^\top b=0\). Put \(D=\sum_{v\in V:b_v>0}b_v\). Add a source \(s\), a sink \(t\), arcs \(s\to v\) fixed at flow \(-b_v\) for nodes with \(b_v<0\), and arcs \(v\to t\) fixed at flow \(b_v\) for nodes with \(b_v>0\). Then homogeneous conservation at every original node is equivalent to \(Bx=b\), and the added arcs carry total \(s\)-to-\(t\) value \(D\). Restriction to the original arcs and extension by the fixed terminal arcs are mutually inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the entering-positive incidence convention, a super-source feeds nodes with negative prescribed net inflow and nodes with positive prescribed net inflow feed a super-sink; the fixed terminal flows yield an equivalent source-sink model of value D.

children.title: Equivalence-Preserving Network Transformations
children.top_down_role: Preservation of feasibility, objective values, and recoverability across network forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence-Preserving Network Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for an exact reduction between network-flow LP formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(P'\) be feasible sets of two network-flow LPs with objectives \(c^\top x\) and \({c'}^\top x'\). A transformation is equivalence-preserving when computable maps \(T:P\to P'\) and \(S:P'\to P\) satisfy \(S(T(x))=x\), \(T(S(x'))=x'\), and \[{c'}^\top T(x)=c^\top x+\gamma\] for a constant \(\gamma\) independent of \(x\). Under these conditions feasibility, infeasibility, optimal solutions, and objective gaps correspond exactly; integrality is also preserved when both maps send integral flows to integral flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network transformation is exact when inverse feasible-flow maps preserve objectives up to a constant; integer equivalence additionally requires integral maps.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and \(S\) are mutually inverse on the feasible sets.
The objective shift \(\gamma\) is solution-independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is optimal in \(P\) exactly when \(T(x)\) is optimal in \(P'\), with values differing by \(\gamma\).

children.title: Uncapacitated Minimum-Cost Flow
children.top_down_role: Minimum-cost flow models without finite arc upper bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\).
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), and \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) is the uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem.

notation.meaning: Node-arc incidence matrix, with one fixed sign convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), let \(B\) be its node-arc incidence matrix under a fixed sign convention. For arc costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) and node supplies \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), the uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}} c^\top x \quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=b,\qquad x\ge 0.
\]
The adjective uncapacitated means that no finite upper bound is imposed on any component \(x_a\); feasibility is determined solely by flow balance and nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize total linear arc cost over nonnegative flows satisfying every node's supply-demand balance, without imposing finite arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncapacitated Minimum-Cost Flow

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of Integral Optima for Uncapacitated Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate primal and dual integrality conclusions for an uncapacitated network-flow problem with finite optimal cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an uncapacitated network-flow problem whose optimal cost is finite. If all supplies \(b_i\) are integers, then there exists an integral optimal flow vector. If all cost coefficients \(c_{ij}\) are integers, then there exists an integral optimal solution of the dual problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an uncapacitated network-flow problem with finite optimal cost, integer supplies guarantee the existence of an integer optimal flow, while integer costs guarantee the existence of an integer optimal dual solution.
assumptions_latex: \text{The network-flow problem is uncapacitated.}
\text{The optimal cost is finite.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall i,\ b_i\in\mathbb Z\right)\Rightarrow\exists\text{ an integral optimal flow};\qquad \left(\forall(i,j),\ c_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\right)\Rightarrow\exists\text{ an integral optimal dual solution}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of uncapacitated minimum-cost flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual formulation of an uncapacitated minimum-cost network-flow LP using node potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem \(\min\{\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\mathbf f:\mathbf A\mathbf f=\mathbf b,\ \mathbf f\ge 0\}\), the dual problem is \(\max\{\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b:\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}\mathbf A\le \mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\}\). When the incidence-matrix column for arc \((i,j)\) yields \(p_i-p_j\), its dual constraint is \(p_i-p_j\le c_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual maximizes the supply-weighted node potentials subject to each arc's potential difference being at most its cost.

children.title: Bounded Minimum-Cost Flow
children.top_down_role: Minimum-cost flow models with lower and upper arc bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite, with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\).
\(c,l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), \(l\le u\), and \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) is the bounded minimum-cost flow problem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-commodity linear-cost flow with explicit lower and upper arc bounds.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\). Given costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), balances \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), and arc bounds \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfying \(l\le u\) and \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), the bounded minimum-cost flow problem is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}} c^\top x \quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=b,\qquad l\le x\le u.
\]
Lower bounds may be eliminated by writing \(x=l+y\), which gives \(By=b-Bl\) and \(0\le y\le u-l\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize linear arc cost subject to node balances and componentwise lower and upper bounds on every arc flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Minimum-Cost Flow

children.title: Minimum-Cost Circulation
children.top_down_role: Circulation models serving as a common representation for costed network flow.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(B\) is its node-arc incidence matrix.
\(c,l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(l\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c^\top x:Bx=0,\ l\le x\le u\}\) defines minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded linear-cost circulation and its standard reduction from balanced minimum-cost flow.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph with incidence matrix \(B\), costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), and bounds \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfying \(l\le u\), minimum-cost circulation is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}} c^\top x \quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=0,\qquad l\le x\le u.
\]
A bounded minimum-cost flow instance \(Bx=b\), where \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), can be represented as circulation by adding an auxiliary node and arcs whose prescribed flows encode the components of \(b\). Feasibility and objective values are preserved after assigning zero cost to the auxiliary arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-cost circulation has zero net balance at every node; balanced supply-demand flow can be represented by adding auxiliary arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Circulation

children.title: Shortest-Path LP Interface
children.top_down_role: Compact and path-based LP representations, potential duality, and the negative-cycle boundary.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph, \(s,t\in V\), and the arc-length vector is \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\).
At least one directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists in \(G\).
The graph contains no negative-cost directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unit-flow primal value, the node-potential dual value, and the minimum \(s\)-to-\(t\) path length are equal.

notation.meaning: Node-arc incidence matrix whose arc columns have positive entries at tails and negative entries at heads.
Set of directed simple paths from s to t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-flow primal, node-potential dual, path-column representation, and the negative-cycle boundary for the unrestricted arc-flow LP.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Shortest Path Problems p. 51

source_refs.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix the incidence convention under which \(Bx=e_s-e_t\) describes one unit sent from \(s\) to \(t\). If at least one directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists and \(G\) contains no negative-cost directed cycle, then
\[
\min\{c^\top x:Bx=e_s-e_t,\ x\ge 0\}
=
\max\{\pi_s-\pi_t:B^\top\pi\le c\}.
\]
The common value is the minimum length of a directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path. If \(\mathcal P_{st}\) is the finite set of directed simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths and \(c(P)=\sum_{a\in P}c_a\), the same value is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}c(P)y_P:\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}y_P=1,\ y_P\ge0\text{ for every }P\in\mathcal P_{st}\right\}.
\]
When an \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists, any negative-cost directed cycle anywhere in \(G\) makes the unrestricted unit-flow arc LP unbounded below, because an arbitrary nonnegative circulation can be added on that cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an s-to-t path exists and the graph has no negative-cost directed cycle, the unit-flow LP, its node-potential dual, and the path-column formulation all have the shortest-path value. Any negative-cost directed cycle makes the unrestricted feasible arc-flow LP unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path LP Interface

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite, \(s\ne t\), and capacities satisfy \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\).
Flow variables are continuous; integrality additionally assumes \(u\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum flow value equals the minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut capacity; integral capacities admit an integral optimum.

notation.meaning: Capacity of arcs leaving a cut set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard directed maximum-flow LP, cut duality, and integral-capacity consequence.

source_refs.locator: 7.5. The maximum flow problem p. 301
3.3.2 A Price-Based Max-Flow Algorithm p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For capacities \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\), maximum flow is the LP
\[
\max F\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=F(e_s-e_t),\qquad 0\le x\le u,
\]
using the convention that \(Bx=F(e_s-e_t)\) sends value \(F\) from \(s\) to \(t\). Its optimal value satisfies
\[
\max F=\min\{u(\delta^+(S)):S\subseteq V,\ s\in S,\ t\notin S\}.
\]
Thus an optimal cut certifies the flow value. If \(u\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{A}\), the LP has an optimal flow \(x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{A}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flow is a capacitated network LP; its value equals a minimum cut capacity, and integral capacities permit an integral optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Flow LP Interface

children.title: Transshipment Models
children.top_down_role: Supply, demand, and intermediate-transfer network models and their reduction to minimum-cost flow.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite, with costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) and capacities \(u\in(\mathbb{R}_{+}\cup\{+\infty\})^{A}\).
Node balances satisfy \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) and \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A transshipment model is the minimum-cost flow LP \(\min\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\).

notation.meaning: Net supply, demand, or zero-transfer balance at each node.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-commodity supply, demand, and intermediate-transfer formulation.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Network Flow Models - Examples p. 8
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: 9.1 The Minimal Cost Network Flow Problem p. 453

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b_v>0\) denote supply, \(b_v<0\) demand, and \(b_v=0\) a pure transshipment node, with \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). Under a compatible incidence convention, the linear transshipment model is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}} c^\top x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=b,\qquad 0\le x\le u.
\]
This is a bounded minimum-cost flow instance. Multiple supply and demand nodes may alternatively be reduced to a single-source, single-sink network by adding a supersource and supersink with zero-cost arcs whose capacities encode the supplies and demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transshipment minimizes routing cost while supplies, demands, and zero-balance transfer nodes obey conservation; it is a minimum-cost flow model.
knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multicommodity-flow LP representation and failure of integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Commodity-specific flow-conservation systems are coupled through shared arc capacities; the resulting continuous LP need not possess an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multicommodity-flow model assigns each commodity $k$ a flow vector $x^k$ satisfying $Ax^k=b^k$ and couples the vectors by $\sum_k x_a^k\le u_a$ for every arc $a$. Although this continuous model is a linear program, integrality need not hold. For the unit-capacity directed three-cycle with path-flow variables $f_1,f_2,f_3$, the feasible set is $f_1+f_3\le1$, $f_1+f_2\le1$, $f_2+f_3\le1$, and $f\ge0$. Its continuous optimum is $3/2$, attained at $f_1=f_2=f_3=1/2$, whereas its integer optimum is $1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multicommodity-flow LP uses a separate flow vector and conservation equations for each commodity while coupling the commodities through shared arc capacities. On the unit-capacity directed three-cycle in the extract, routing one half unit of each commodity gives the continuous optimum 3/2, while every integer-feasible routing has total flow at most 1.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is a directed network with capacities }u_a.
Ax^k=b^k,\quad x^k\ge0\quad\text{for every commodity }k.
\sum_k x_a^k\le u_a\quad\text{for every arc }a.
\text{In the counterexample, all three arcs have capacity }1\text{ and each commodity is restricted to its specified two-arc path.}

children.title: Arc-Based Multicommodity Models
children.top_down_role: Commodity-indexed compact formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and commodities are indexed by a finite set \(K\).
Each commodity \(k\) has balance vector \(b^k\) with \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v^k=0\), and shared capacities satisfy \(u\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compact multicommodity LP uses arc variables \(x_a^k\) with commodity balances and shared inequalities \(\sum_k x_a^k\le u_a\).

notation.meaning: Flow of commodity k on arc a.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact linear formulation with commodity-indexed arc flows and shared capacities.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: 6. Large scale optimization p. 231

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite commodity set \(K\), let \(x^k\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\) be commodity \(k\)'s arc flow, \(b^k\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) its balance vector, and \(c^k\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) its arc costs. The arc-based multicommodity model is
\[
\min \sum_{k\in K}(c^k)^\top x^k
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
Bx^k=b^k\ \text{for every }k\in K,
\qquad \sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\ \text{for every }a\in A,
\qquad x^k\ge0.
\]
The balance constraints are commodity-separable; only the shared arc-capacity inequalities couple commodities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each commodity has its own arc-flow and balance equations, while total flow across commodities is limited by shared arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Based Multicommodity Models

children.title: Path-Based Multicommodity Models
children.top_down_role: Route-column formulations connected to delayed column generation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph and \(K\) is a finite commodity set.

Each \(k\in K\) has origin \(s_k\), destination \(t_k\), demand \(d_k\ge0\), nonnegative arc costs \(c^k\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\), and path set \(\mathcal P_k\) containing all directed simple \(s_k\)-to-\(t_k\) paths.
Shared arc capacities satisfy \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The path-flow LP has one explicitly quantified demand equation per commodity and one explicitly quantified shared-capacity inequality per arc, and it has the same optimal value as the corresponding nonnegative-cost arc-flow model.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative flow assigned to path P of commodity k.
Set of all directed simple origin-destination paths for commodity k.
Indicator equal to one when arc a belongs to path P and zero otherwise.
Sum of commodity-k arc costs along path P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Route-column formulation for splittable multicommodity flow with nonnegative arc costs and all simple origin-destination paths available as columns.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: 6. Large scale optimization p. 231

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(k\in K\), let \(\mathcal P_k\) contain all directed simple \(s_k\)-to-\(t_k\) paths, let \(y_P^k\ge0\) be the flow assigned to \(P\in\mathcal P_k\), and define \(\delta_{aP}=1\) if \(a\in P\) and \(\delta_{aP}=0\) otherwise. For nonnegative arc costs \(c^k\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\), define \(c_P^k=\sum_{a\in A}c_a^k\delta_{aP}\). The path-based splittable multicommodity formulation is
\[
\min \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}c_P^k y_P^k
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}y_P^k=d_k\quad\text{for every }k\in K,
\]
\[
\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}\delta_{aP}y_P^k\le u_a
\quad\text{for every }a\in A,
\qquad
y_P^k\ge0\quad\text{for every }k\in K\text{ and }P\in\mathcal P_k.
\]
Arc flows are recovered by \(x_a^k=\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}\delta_{aP}y_P^k\). Conversely, flow decomposition and removal of nonnegative-cost cycles show that this formulation has the same optimal value as the corresponding arc-flow model. Delayed column generation may introduce path columns only when needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For splittable commodities with nonnegative arc costs, demand is assigned to origin-destination path columns, shared arc capacities couple those columns, and the route formulation has the same optimal value as the corresponding arc-flow model.
knowledge_statements.title: Path-Based Multicommodity Models

children.title: Shared-Capacity Coupling
children.top_down_role: The linking structure separating multicommodity flow from independent single-commodity models.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is finite and each \(x^k\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\) satisfies its own commodity-balance equations.
Shared capacities satisfy \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraints \(\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\) are the linking rows that prevent commoditywise decomposition.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative multiplier for arc a's shared capacity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linking-row structure in splittable multicommodity flow.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: 6. Large scale optimization p. 231

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In an arc-based multicommodity LP, each commodity's balance constraints involve only \(x^k\), whereas every capacitated arc contributes the linking inequality
\[
\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a.
\]
Without these inequalities, the feasible region is the Cartesian product of the single-commodity feasible regions and a separable linear objective decomposes by commodity. With them, commodities compete for capacity. Assigning multipliers \(\lambda_a\ge0\) to the linking inequalities produces commoditywise subproblems with modified arc costs \(c_a^k+\lambda_a\), plus the constant term \(-\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a u_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared arc-capacity rows couple otherwise independent commodity flows; dualizing them separates the problem into commodity subproblems with adjusted arc costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Capacity Coupling

Prescribed net generalized supply at node v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear generalized-flow convention where an arc multiplies flow between its tail and head.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A generalized flow network assigns each directed arc \(a=(i,j)\) a gain \(\gamma_a>0\). If \(x_a\ge0\) units leave node \(i\) on arc \(a\), then \(\gamma_a x_a\) units arrive at node \(j\). Under the convention that \(b_v\) is generalized net supply at node \(v\), feasibility requires
\[
\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}\gamma_a x_a=b_v
\quad\text{for every }v\in V,
\]
together with any stated arc bounds. Ordinary network flow is the special case \(\gamma_a=1\) for all \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized-flow arc multiplies transmitted flow by a positive gain, so node balance uses gain-adjusted inflow rather than ordinary conservation.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Flow Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generalized-flow convention and node-balance formula are mathematically coherent and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but no source record or inspectable locator is supplied. children.title: Time-Expanded Networks
children.top_down_role: Temporally layered network representations for dynamic flow decisions.

assumptions_latex: The original dynamic network has finite vertex set \(V\) and discrete times \(T=\{0,\ldots,H\}\).
Each admissible movement or waiting action has a specified departure time and nonnegative integer transit time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dynamic flow is represented as static flow on time-state vertices \((v,t)\) and temporally admissible arcs.

notation.meaning: Time-state copy of vertex v at time t.
Integer transit time of original arc a.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon, discrete-time expansion of a dynamic network into a static directed network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a discrete horizon \(T=\{0,\ldots,H\}\), the time-expanded network has vertex set
\[
V^T=\{(v,t):v\in V,\ t\in T\}.
\]
An original arc \(a=(i,j)\) with transit time \(\tau_a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) induces an arc from \((i,t)\) to \((j,t+\tau_a)\) whenever \(t+\tau_a\le H\). Waiting may be represented by arcs from \((v,t)\) to \((v,t+1)\). Capacities, costs, supplies, and demands indexed by time are assigned to the corresponding copies. Static flow conservation at each time-state vertex then represents dynamic conservation and temporal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicate each vertex by time, connect only temporally feasible movements and waits, and solve the resulting dynamic-flow model as a static network LP.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Expanded Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-horizon discrete-time expansion is a precise standard representation and its content kind fits the leaf. However, the record provides no citation or locator supporting the construction and its modeling correspondence.

children.title: Gain-Loss Conservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conservation structures altered by amplification, attenuation, or transformation factors.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and every arc \(a=(i,j)\) has gain \(\gamma_a>0\).
Flow \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\) satisfies the generalized node-balance equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total ordinary flow is conserved only when the gain-induced change \(\sum_a(\gamma_a-1)x_a\) is compatible with total prescribed imbalance.

notation.meaning: Positive gain or loss factor on arc a.
Prescribed generalized net supply at node v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate balance identity distinguishing ordinary conservation from gain-loss conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose generalized balance is written as
\[
\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}\gamma_a x_a=b_v
\quad\text{for every }v\in V.
\]
Summing these equations over all nodes yields the necessary identity
\[
\sum_{v\in V}b_v=\sum_{a\in A}(1-\gamma_a)x_a.
\]
Hence the ordinary zero-sum condition \(\sum_v b_v=0\) is not sufficient by itself when gains differ from one. Arcs with \(\gamma_a>1\) create flow in the aggregate accounting, arcs with \(0<\gamma_a<1\) lose flow, and ordinary conservation is recovered when every \(\gamma_a=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summed generalized balances expose aggregate creation or loss: ordinary zero-sum conservation returns only when gains are one or their effects cancel.
knowledge_statements.title: Gain-Loss Conservation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aggregate identity follows consistently from the stated generalized balances, and the property content kind is appropriate for the gain-loss regime leaf. No authoritative source or specific locator is supplied, so the candidate must remain source-blocked.

children.title: Temporal-Layering Size Boundary
children.top_down_role: Representation growth and sparsity consequences created by time expansion.

knowledge_statements.title: Temporal-Layering Size Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size and encoding boundary for a finite-horizon time-expanded network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the horizon be \(T\in\mathbb Z_{+}\), and let each arc \(a\in A\) have integral transit time \(\tau_a\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\). The time-expanded graph has \((T+1)|V|\) time-layered nodes, \(|V|T\) waiting arcs, and \(\sum_{a\in A}(T-\tau_a+1)\) transit arcs. Thus its explicit construction and any algorithm polynomial in the expanded graph size are polynomial in \(|V|+|A|+T\). If \(T\) is encoded in binary, this bound is generally pseudopolynomial rather than polynomial in the input bit length, because the expansion may have size exponential in \(\log T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Time expansion is linear in the numeric horizon but can be exponentially larger than its binary encoding, so expanded-network algorithms are generally pseudopolynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(T\) and all \(\tau_a\) are nonnegative integers.
A waiting arc is included between consecutive copies of every node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V_T|=(T+1)|V|\) and \(|A_T|=|V|T+\sum_{a\in A}(T-\tau_a+1)\), giving a pseudopolynomial boundary under binary encoding of \(T\).

knowledge_statements.title: Node Potential Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual node variables for the bounded minimum-cost flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), a node-potential system is a vector \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) assigned to the balance equations \(Bx=b\). With each arc column having \(+1\) at its tail and \(-1\) at its head, an arc \(a=(i,j)\) has potential difference \((B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_a=\pi_i-\pi_j\). If \(\mathcal C\) is the set of weakly connected components and \(z=\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}\alpha_C\mathbf 1_C\), then \(B^{\mathsf T}(\pi+z)=B^{\mathsf T}\pi\). Thus one representative can be selected by fixing one root potential in each component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node potentials are dual variables for flow-balance equations. Only potential differences affect arc conditions, so one potential per weakly connected component may be normalized.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(B\) uses the tail-positive, head-negative incidence convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_{ij}=\pi_i-\pi_j\), and the potential vector is determined only up to an additive constant on each weakly connected component.

notation.meaning: indicator vector of weakly connected component C

knowledge_statements.title: Arc Reduced-Cost Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced costs induced by node potentials in a bounded minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\), where each incidence column for \(a=(i,j)\) is tail-positive and head-negative. For \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\), define the reduced cost by \[r_a=c_a-(B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_a=c_a-\pi_i+\pi_j.\] For every flow satisfying \(Bx=b\), \(c^{\mathsf T}x=r^{\mathsf T}x+\pi^{\mathsf T}b\). Consequently, objective differences between balance-feasible flows equal the corresponding reduced-cost differences, and componentwise constant shifts of \(\pi\) leave \(r\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc's reduced cost is its original cost minus the tail-to-head potential difference. This transformation preserves objective comparisons among balance-feasible flows.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(Bx=b\) uses the tail-positive incidence convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r=c-B^{\mathsf T}\pi\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=r^{\mathsf T}x+\pi^{\mathsf T}b\) whenever \(Bx=b\).

notation.meaning: original unit cost of arc a

knowledge_statements.title: Potential–Cost Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential characterization of residual-cycle optimality for minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\). Its residual graph contains a forward residual arc of cost \(c_a\) when \(x_a<u_a\) and a reverse residual arc of cost \(-c_a\) when \(x_a>l_a\). The residual graph has no negative-cost directed cycle if and only if there exists \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) such that every residual arc \((i,j)\), with residual cost \(d_{ij}\), satisfies \[d_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\ge 0.\] Thus cycle nonnegativity and feasible reduced-cost potentials are equivalent optimality certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow has no negative residual cycle exactly when node potentials make every residual arc's reduced cost nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: The bounded minimum-cost flow instance is finite.
\(x\) satisfies \(Bx=b\) and \(l\le x\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No negative-cost residual cycle exists if and only if \(d_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\ge0\) for every residual arc and some \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Sign Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary-slackness signs for lower, interior, and upper arc states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\), assume \(l_a<u_a\) for every arc and let \(r=c-B^{\mathsf T}\pi\). A feasible flow \(x\) and potential vector \(\pi\) satisfy the reduced-cost sign condition when, for every arc \(a\), \[x_a=l_a\Rightarrow r_a\ge0,\qquad l_a<x_a<u_a\Rightarrow r_a=0,\qquad x_a=u_a\Rightarrow r_a\le0.\] These conditions are equivalent to nonnegative reduced costs on every residual arc. Their satisfaction certifies global optimality of \(x\); conversely, finite-dimensional LP duality supplies such potentials for every optimal feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For arcs with distinct lower and upper bounds, lower-bound arcs require nonnegative reduced cost, interior arcs zero reduced cost, and upper-bound arcs nonpositive reduced cost. These signs characterize optimality.
assumptions_latex: The network and all data are finite.
\(l_a<u_a\) for every arc \(a\in A\).
The bounded flow problem has a feasible flow with finite objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign regimes hold for some \(\pi\) if and only if every residual reduced cost is nonnegative, and in that case \(x\) is optimal.

children.title: Cut-Capacity Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Capacity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificate bounding an ordinary source-to-sink flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be an \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(v\) in a directed network with capacities \(0\le x_a\le u_a\). For every set \(S\subseteq V\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), flow balance gives \[v=x(\delta^+(S))-x(\delta^-(S))\le u(\delta^+(S)).\] Therefore the set \(S\), together with the listed crossing capacities, is a directly checkable certificate that no feasible flow can exceed \(u(\delta^+(S))\). If a feasible flow attains this value, the flow and cut jointly certify maximum-flow optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every source–sink cut bounds feasible flow value by its outgoing capacity; equality between a flow and cut certifies maximum-flow optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed network.
\(x\) obeys capacity constraints and flow conservation outside \(s,t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\le u(\delta^+(S))\); equality certifies that \(x\) is maximum and \(S\) is a minimum cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Balance Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A violated cut inequality certifying infeasibility of bounded balance equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(Bx=b\) with \(l\le x\le u\), using the tail-positive incidence convention, and assume \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), each feasible flow satisfies \[b(S)=x(\delta^+(S))-x(\delta^-(S))\le u(\delta^+(S))-l(\delta^-(S)).\] Hence any set \(S\) satisfying \(b(S)>u(\delta^+(S))-l(\delta^-(S))\) is a finite, verifiable infeasibility certificate. Applying the inequality to \(V\setminus S\) yields the corresponding lower attainable cut-balance test.

\(l_a\le u_a\) for every arc \(a\in A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Flow Minimum-Cut Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality between the optimal source–sink flow value and the minimum capacity of a separating directed cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and nonnegative arc capacities \(k_{ij}\). Then
\[
\max_{x\in\mathcal F_{s,t}} |x|
=
\min_{\substack{S\subseteq V:\ s\in S,\ t\notin S}}
\sum_{(i,j)\in\delta^+(S)} k_{ij},
\qquad
\delta^+(S)=\{(i,j)\in A:i\in S,\ j\notin S\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite capacitated directed network, the greatest feasible flow from the source to the sink equals the least capacity of any directed cut separating them.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is a finite directed network with source }s\text{ and sink }t.
k_{ij}\ge 0\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in A.
\mathcal F_{s,t}\text{ consists of flows satisfying arc-capacity bounds and flow conservation at every node other than }s,t.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{x\in\mathcal F_{s,t}}|x|=\min_{S:\,s\in S,\,t\notin S}\sum_{(i,j)\in\delta^+(S)}k_{ij}.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Tree-Basis Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spanning-tree representation of bases for a connected bounded network LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have connected underlying undirected graph. Delete one row from its node-arc incidence matrix and the corresponding entry from \(b\), obtaining \(\bar B\) and \(\bar b\). A set \(T\subseteq A\) of \(|V|-1\) columns forms a nonsingular basis \(\bar B_T\) if and only if the undirected arcs underlying \(T\) form a spanning tree. In a bounded network basic solution, every nonbasic arc is assigned to one of its bounds; once those assignments are fixed, the tree-arc flows are uniquely determined by \(\bar Bx=\bar b\). Adding one nonbasic arc to \(T\) creates a unique fundamental cycle, while deleting one tree arc partitions the tree and determines a fundamental cut. These structures organize a network-simplex pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced incidence-matrix bases correspond to spanning trees. Once nonbasic arcs are fixed at bounds, tree flows are unique, and fundamental cycles and cuts organize network-simplex pivots.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Simplex Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common pivot template encompassing primal, dual, and bounded-arc network simplex variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite bounded minimum-cost flow instance and a tree basis with arc states. In the primal variant, maintain primal feasibility, compute tree potentials, select a nonbasic arc violating its bound-appropriate reduced-cost sign, augment on its fundamental cycle to the first blocking bound, exchange arcs, and stop when all signs are valid. In the dual variant, maintain dual reduced-cost feasibility, select a primal-infeasible tree arc, use its fundamental cut to choose an entering arc by a dual ratio test, pivot, and stop when primal feasibility is restored. Bounded-arc variants record each nonbasic arc at its lower or upper bound; strongly feasible variants impose an orientation or tie-breaking rule preventing degenerate cycling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network simplex variants share tree pivots but preserve different invariants: primal feasibility, dual feasibility, bounded-arc states, or strong-feasibility rules.
assumptions_latex: The network LP is finite and has a tree-basis representation.
A valid initial basis for the chosen variant is available.
Pivot ties follow a finite anti-cycling rule when necessary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On termination with both primal feasibility and valid reduced-cost signs, the current tree solution is optimal.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Tree Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization of a bounded minimum-cost flow from a directly available feasible spanning-tree basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a connected directed network, balances \(b_i\) satisfying \(\sum_i b_i=0\), and bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\), choose a spanning tree \(T\). Assign every arc outside \(T\) to either \(\ell_a\) or \(u_a\), then uniquely determine the tree-arc flows from \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(i)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(i)}x_a=b_i\). If every resulting tree flow satisfies \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\), initialize the network-simplex basis with \(T\), the computed flows, and node potentials satisfying zero reduced cost on tree arcs. Otherwise this tree and bound assignment do not provide an initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix non-tree arcs at bounds and solve flow balance uniquely on a spanning tree. The resulting basis is usable exactly when all tree flows respect their bounds.

\(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\).
\(T\subseteq A\) is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in T\) implies that the constructed tree solution is primal feasible.

children.title: Artificial-Arc Initialization

knowledge_statements.title: Artificial-Arc Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-I star-tree initialization for a balanced minimum-cost flow problem lacking an obvious feasible tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be an underlying-undirected connected network with shifted balances \(b_i\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\), zero shifted lower bounds, and shifted arc capacities. Introduce an artificial root \(r\). Initialize every original arc at zero; for each \(i\in V\) with \(b_i>0\), add an artificial arc \((i,r)\) carrying \(b_i\), and for each \(i\in V\) with \(b_i<0\), add an artificial arc \((r,i)\) carrying \(-b_i\). These artificial arcs form a feasible star-tree basis. In Phase I, assign cost one to artificial arcs and cost zero to original arcs and minimize \(\sum_{a\in A_{\mathrm{art}}}x_a\). The shifted original network is feasible if and only if the Phase-I optimum is zero. At a zero optimum, pivot zero-flow artificial basic arcs out whenever possible and perform basis cleanup to obtain a possibly degenerate feasible original-network tree basis; a positive optimum certifies infeasibility of the shifted original network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A root and artificial arcs create a feasible star basis. Minimizing total artificial flow gives a zero optimum exactly when the shifted original network is feasible; zero-flow artificial basic arcs then require basis cleanup before removal.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is connected after orientations are ignored.
\(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\).
Original lower bounds have been shifted to zero.
Artificial arcs have capacity at least their initialized flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\sum_{a\in A_{\mathrm{art}}}x_a=0\) if and only if the original shifted network has a feasible flow.

notation.meaning: shifted node balance under the outflow-minus-inflow convention

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Artificial-arc initialization for network simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a Phase-I transshipment problem with an explicit feasible tree and classifies its optimal outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\sum_{k\in V}b_k=0$ and choose $w\in V$. For every $j\ne w$ with $b_j\ge0$, use or add arc $wj$, and for every $i\ne w$ with $b_i<0$, use or add arc $iw$. These $|V|-1$ arcs form a tree $T_w$, and setting $x_{wj}=b_j$, $x_{iw}=-b_i$, and $x_{ij}=0$ off $T_w$ gives a feasible flow in the enlarged network. Assign $p_{ij}=1$ to artificial arcs and $p_{ij}=0$ to original arcs, and minimize $\sum_{ij}p_{ij}x_{ij}$. A positive optimum certifies infeasibility of the original network. If an optimal tree has no artificial arc, its flow and tree initialize the original problem. If all artificial arcs have zero flow but some remain in the optimal tree, the original problem is feasible but may have no feasible tree solution. Separately, if no tree is visited more than once, network simplex terminates because the number of trees is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete a rooted star with artificial arcs to obtain an explicit feasible tree, then minimize total flow on artificial arcs. A positive optimum certifies original infeasibility; an optimal tree without artificial arcs initializes the original problem; zero-flow artificial tree arcs establish feasibility but may indicate that no feasible original tree exists. Absence of repeated trees also guarantees finite termination.
assumptions_latex: $G=(V,A)$ is a transshipment network with $\sum_{k\in V}b_k=0$.
Flows are nonnegative and satisfy $\sum_i x_{ik}-\sum_jx_{kj}=b_k$ for every $k\in V$.
For the termination assertion, each tree is visited in at most one iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\sum_{ij}p_{ij}x_{ij}>0\iff\text{the original problem is infeasible},\qquad \min\sum_{ij}p_{ij}x_{ij}=0\iff\text{the original problem is feasible}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: All-Artificial Rooted-Tree Initialization for Network Simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a feasible artificial starting basis for a network-structured nonnegative equality-form linear program; subsequent Phase I or Big-M processing tests, but does not guarantee, feasibility of the original system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:A^0x=b,\ x\geq0\}\), where \(A^0\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and each column is either a signed unit vector or has exactly one \(+1\), one \(-1\), and otherwise zeros. For each row define \(s_i=1\) if \(b_i\geq0\) and \(s_i=-1\) otherwise, and add the artificial column \(s_i e_i\). Append a redundant row equal to the negative sum of the extended rows, thereby introducing a new graph node \(m+1\); designate it as the root and add the root column \(e_{m+1}\). The \(m\) artificial arcs and the root arc form a rooted spanning-tree basis, with artificial values \(x_{a,i}=|b_i|\) and root-arc value zero, that is feasible for the augmented system. From this basis, apply either Phase I or Big-\(M\). If feasibility of the original system is attained, delete nonbasic artificial arcs and temporarily retain any degenerate basic artificial arcs with Big-\(M\) costs while optimization continues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative network-structured equality-form linear program, add one signed artificial unit column per row, choosing the positive sign when the corresponding right-hand side is zero or positive. Add a redundant negative row sum to create a new root node, then add a root arc. The artificial arcs together with the root arc form a feasible rooted-tree basis for the augmented problem. Phase I or Big-M can then seek feasibility of the original system; feasibility is not guaranteed. If it is attained, remove nonbasic artificial arcs and temporarily retain degenerate basic artificial arcs with Big-M costs.
assumptions_latex: A^0\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
x\geq0
\forall j,\ A^0_{:j}\text{ is a signed unit column or has exactly one }+1\text{ and one }-1
A^0x=b\text{ is the network-structured equality system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The augmented system has a feasible rooted-spanning-tree basis consisting of the }m\text{ artificial arcs and one root arc; Phase I or Big-}M\text{ may then determine whether original feasibility can be attained.}

children.title: Candidate-Arc Pricing
children.top_down_role: Selection of nonbasic arcs as pivot candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate-Arc Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal network-simplex eligibility condition for a nonbasic arc at one of its bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, let \(a=(i,j)\) be nonbasic and define its reduced cost by \(\bar c_a=c_a+\pi_i-\pi_j\). The arc is an improving entering candidate when either \(x_a=\ell_a\) and \(\bar c_a<0\), so increasing it can improve the objective, or \(x_a=u_a\) and \(\bar c_a>0\), so decreasing it can improve the objective. Pricing may select any eligible arc, commonly one maximizing \(-\bar c_a\) at a lower bound or \(\bar c_a\) at an upper bound. Absence of every such candidate establishes reduced-cost optimality of the current feasible tree solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-bound arc is eligible when its reduced cost is negative; an upper-bound arc is eligible when it is positive. No eligible arc means optimality.
assumptions_latex: The current tree solution is primal feasible.
Tree potentials satisfy \(c_a+\pi_i-\pi_j=0\) on every tree arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x_a=\ell_a,\ \bar c_a<0\}\lor\{x_a=u_a,\ \bar c_a>0\}\) is the entering-candidate condition.

children.title: Partial-Pricing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Candidate searches restricted to subsets or scheduled groups of arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Pricing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise reduced-cost search that avoids scanning every nonbasic arc before each network-simplex pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the nonbasic arcs into blocks \(P_1,\ldots,P_q\) and maintain a cyclic block index. Scan the current block, compute reduced costs, and retain arcs satisfying the entering condition. If candidates occur, select one according to the prescribed rule and pivot; otherwise advance to the next block. After a pivot, update the basis, flows, potentials, and affected candidate information before continuing. Declare optimality only after a complete scan of all blocks, using potentials valid for the current basis, finds no eligible arc. Thus partial pricing changes the search schedule but not the reduced-cost optimality test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan nonbasic arcs block by block and pivot when a block yields an eligible arc. Optimality requires a candidate-free full sweep for the unchanged current basis.
assumptions_latex: \(A\setminus T=P_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}P_q\).
Reduced costs are recomputed or maintained consistently after each pivot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A full current-basis sweep with no eligible arc implies reduced-cost optimality.

children.title: Network Simplex Implementation Structure
children.top_down_role: Tree-update data structures and maintenance of flows, potentials, and basis state.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Simplex Implementation Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal coherent state and update dependencies for implementing a primal network-simplex pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An implementation state may be represented by \(S=(T,x,\pi,\sigma,D)\), where \(T\) is the spanning-tree basis, \(x\) contains arc flows, \(\pi\) contains node potentials, \(\sigma\) records each nonbasic arc's lower- or upper-bound status, and \(D\) stores rooted-tree data. Inserting an eligible nonbasic arc creates one fundamental cycle, and the ratio test determines the maximal feasible step. Flows change only along that cycle. If a tree arc limits the step, the entering arc replaces a selected limiting tree arc in \(T\), bound statuses are updated, the rooted-tree data are repaired, and potentials are shifted on one resulting tree component to restore zero reduced costs on tree arcs. If the entering arc reaches its opposite bound before any tree arc limits the step, \(T\) is unchanged and only its bound status and the affected flow are updated. In either case, the next state must preserve balance, bounds, bound-status consistency, and the tree reduced-cost equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maintained state comprises the tree, flows, potentials, nonbasic bound statuses, and rooted-tree data. A pivot updates one fundamental cycle and either exchanges a limiting tree arc or performs a bound flip, while restoring all invariants.
assumptions_latex: The current state represents a primal-feasible tree solution.
The entering nonbasic arc satisfies the reduced-cost eligibility condition.
The ratio test includes both tree-arc limits and the opposite bound of the entering arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The updated state \(S'\) preserves node balance, flow bounds, a spanning-tree basis, consistent nonbasic bound statuses, and zero reduced costs on tree arcs.

children.title: Network Simplex Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate tree bases and zero-improvement pivots in network simplex.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Simplex Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of a primal network-simplex tree solution and of an individual pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible network-simplex tree solution is degenerate when at least one basic tree arc is at a flow bound. For a particular eligible entering arc, the associated pivot is degenerate when the fundamental-cycle ratio test gives maximal feasible step \(\theta=0\). A degenerate tree solution does not necessarily make every proposed pivot degenerate; the zero-step condition depends on the direction of cycle augmentation and the limiting arcs. A degenerate pivot may exchange the entering and leaving arcs without changing the flow vector or objective value. Degeneracy does not itself imply cycling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree solution is degenerate when a basic tree arc is at a bound. A particular pivot is degenerate when its allowable cycle-augmentation step is zero; not every pivot from a degenerate solution must have zero step.
assumptions_latex: The current tree solution satisfies node balance and all arc bounds.
The proposed entering arc has positive bound width and satisfies the pricing eligibility condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a proposed entering arc, \(\theta=0\) characterizes a degenerate pivot, whereas a basic tree arc at a bound characterizes a degenerate tree solution.

notation.meaning: maximum feasible cycle-augmentation step for the proposed entering arc

children.title: Network Simplex Cycling
children.top_down_role: Basis repetition and anti-cycling concerns in network pivot sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Simplex Cycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated-basis nontermination caused by a sequence of degenerate network-simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Network-simplex cycling occurs when, without reaching a stopping condition, the algorithm returns to a previously visited complete basis state: the same spanning tree together with the same lower- or upper-bound statuses of all nonbasic arcs. Because the pivot rule is deterministic from that state, the subsequent sequence then repeats indefinitely. Every pivot on such a cycle has zero objective improvement; in the standard primal method this requires degeneracy. A finite anti-cycling ordering, such as a consistent lexicographic or Bland-type rule, excludes repetition of a complete basis state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cycling is the return to an identical tree and nonbasic bound-status state, causing a deterministic pivot sequence to repeat indefinitely through degenerate pivots.
assumptions_latex: The pivot and tie-breaking rules are deterministic.
Only finitely many complete basis states exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_k=S_ell\) for some \(k<\ell\) implies indefinite repetition unless the pivot rule is changed.

notation.meaning: complete network-simplex basis state after pivot k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Root-orientation anti-cycling criterion for network simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient orientation condition on every degenerate tree exchange that excludes cycling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a root. If, in every degenerate pivot from $T$ to $T+e-f$, the entering arc $e$ is directed away from the root in the new tree $T+e-f$, then the network simplex method does not cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network simplex cannot cycle if every degenerate pivot places its entering arc in the new tree with orientation away from the fixed root.
assumptions_latex: A root is fixed throughout the network-simplex iterations.
For every degenerate pivot $T\mapsto T+e-f$, the entering arc $e$ is directed away from the root in $T+e-f$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The network-simplex tree sequence does not cycle.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degeneracy, stalling, and possible cycling in network simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines network-simplex degeneracy and records both the existence and the stated limits of the cycling example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible tree solution $(T,x)$ is degenerate if $x_{ij}=0$ for some tree arc $ij\in T$. A pivot with leaving arc $f$ is degenerate when $x_f=0$; such a pivot changes the tree but leaves the feasible flow $x$ and its objective value unchanged. Consequently, degenerate pivots can stall. Moreover, there exist transshipment instances and admissible pivot choices for which the network simplex method returns to an earlier tree and can repeat indefinitely without reaching an optimum. This example does not establish whether cycling can occur when every entering arc maximizes $y_j-y_i-c_{ij}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible tree is degenerate when a tree arc has zero flow. A zero-step degenerate pivot changes only the tree, so it can cause stalling. Under some pivot choices, network simplex can return to an earlier tree and cycle indefinitely. The extract leaves open whether this can happen under the maximum-reduced-profit entering rule.
assumptions_latex: $T$ is a spanning-tree basis defining a feasible nonnegative transshipment flow $x$.
No anti-cycling restriction is imposed on the illustrated entering- and leaving-arc choices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Degenerate pivots may stall, and some admissible pivot sequences cycle; cycling is not asserted for every pivot rule.}

children.title: Network Simplex Stalling
children.top_down_role: Extended periods of negligible objective progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Simplex Stalling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite or prolonged absence of objective progress during successive network-simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network-simplex run stalls over a segment containing at least one pivot when its complete basis states change while the objective values satisfy \(z_k=z_{k+1}=\cdots=z_{k+r}\) for some integer \(r\ge1\). If every entering arc in the segment has strictly improving reduced cost and computations use exact arithmetic, each unchanged-objective pivot must have cycle-augmentation step \(\theta=0\) and is degenerate. Without the strict-pricing hypothesis, a positive-step pivot on a zero-reduced-cost arc can also preserve the objective value. Stalling differs from cycling because the visited complete basis states may all be distinct and a later pivot may make objective progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stalling is a sequence of basis changes with unchanged objective value. Under strict improving pricing in exact arithmetic, its pivots are zero-step and degenerate; with zero-reduced-cost pivots allowed, unchanged objective can also accompany a positive step.
assumptions_latex: Objective values and feasibility tests are evaluated in exact arithmetic.
Each iteration performs a valid primal network-simplex pivot.
The zero-step conclusion is asserted only when entering arcs have strictly improving reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_k=\cdots=z_{k+r}\) with \(r\ge1\) and changing complete basis states defines a stalled segment.

notation.meaning: objective value at complete basis state k
positive number of pivots in the stalled segment

children.title: Network Simplex Numerical Stability
children.top_down_role: Finite-precision behavior of potentials, costs, bounds, and feasibility checks.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Simplex Numerical Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision boundary for feasibility, pricing, and ratio-test decisions in network simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In floating-point network simplex, computed flows and potentials generally satisfy balance, bounds, and tree reduced-cost equations only up to residuals. If a true reduced cost or ratio-test separation is comparable to accumulated rounding error, its sign or the leaving arc can be misclassified. Consequently, exact-arithmetic guarantees apply directly only when decision margins exceed certified error bounds. A reliable implementation must use scaled tolerances, residual checks, and periodic recomputation; otherwise it may accept an infeasible flow, miss an improving arc, or perform unstable near-zero pivots. No fixed absolute tolerance is invariant under arbitrary rescaling of costs and capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding can reverse pricing and ratio-test decisions when margins are too small. Scaled tolerances and residual recomputation are necessary; fixed absolute tolerances are not scale invariant.
assumptions_latex: Flows and potentials are stored and updated in finite precision.
Problem data may vary substantially in magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decision reliability requires each tested margin to exceed its associated numerical error bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claims are plausible, but the record makes network-simplex-specific assertions about certified error margins, scaled tolerances, recomputation, and failure modes without any cited source. A numerical analysis or implementation reference with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Network Simplex Worst-Case Complexity
children.top_down_role: Worst-case positioning of network simplex pivot behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Simplex Worst-Case Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial pivot bound for a nonrepeating bounded-arc network-simplex run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a connected network with \(n\) nodes and \(m\) arcs, finite lower and upper bounds, and a pivot rule that never repeats a complete basis state. A state consists of a spanning tree with \(n-1\) basic arcs and a lower- or upper-bound status for each remaining arc. Hence the number of possible states is at most \(\binom{m}{n-1}2^{m-n+1}\), and termination occurs within fewer pivots than this number. This is an exponential combinatorial upper bound, not a polynomial-time guarantee. The total arithmetic cost also depends on the per-pivot tree-update and pricing implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonrepeating run has at most one pivot per tree-and-bound-status state, giving an exponential combinatorial bound and no general polynomial-time guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The underlying undirected network is connected.
Every nonbasic arc is fixed at one of two finite bounds.
The pivot rule prevents repeated complete basis states.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transportation Problems as Bipartite Transshipment Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines transshipment and its bipartite transportation specialization, including necessary node-balance sign conditions for feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network-flow problem interpreted as shipping goods through a transportation network is a transshipment problem. Let \(\mathcal N=\mathcal S\cup\mathcal D\), with \(\mathcal S\cap\mathcal D=\varnothing\), and suppose every arc has its tail in \(\mathcal S\) and its head in \(\mathcal D\). A transshipment problem on this bipartite graph is a transportation problem; \(\mathcal S\) consists of supply nodes and \(\mathcal D\) of demand nodes. Feasibility requires \(b_i\ge 0\) for every \(i\in\mathcal S\) and \(b_i\le 0\) for every \(i\in\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shipment interpretation of a network-flow problem is a transshipment problem. When its nodes split into supply and demand sets and every arc runs from a supply node to a demand node, it is a transportation problem. Feasibility necessarily requires nonnegative supply-node balances and nonpositive demand-node balances.

\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal S\times\mathcal D

children.title: Balanced Transportation Models
