knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Transportation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form transportation LP with equal aggregate supply and demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let origins \(I\) have supplies \(s_i\ge0\), destinations \(J\) have demands \(d_j\ge0\), and shipment costs \(c_{ij}\). A balanced transportation model satisfies \(\sum_{i\in I}s_i=\sum_{j\in J}d_j\) and has the linear program \[\min_{x\ge0}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=s_i\ (i\in I),\qquad \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=d_j\ (j\in J).\] One equality is redundant, and whenever all origin-destination pairs are permitted, the balance identity is sufficient for feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced transportation LP ships every origin's supply and meets every destination's demand, with total supply equal to total demand.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite nonempty sets.
Every pair \((i,j)\in I\times J\) is an allowed shipment arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i s_i=\sum_j d_j\) makes the equality-form complete-bipartite transportation constraints feasible.

notation.meaning: shipment from origin i to destination j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Balanced Transportation LP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete-route balanced transportation formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given supplies $a_i\ge 0$, demands $b_j\ge 0$, and costs $c_{ij}\in\mathbb R$, with $\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=\sum_{j=1}^n b_j$, the classical transportation problem is
\[
\min_{x\ge 0}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=a_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ij}=b_j\ (j=1,\ldots,n).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose nonnegative shipments that exhaust every origin's supply and satisfy every destination's demand while minimizing total shipping cost; aggregate supply and demand are equal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Balanced Transportation Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines direct shipment from fixed supplies to fixed demands, with exact balance constraints and additive linear shipping cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $I$ be a set of sources, $J$ a set of destinations, and $A\subseteq I\times J$ the available direct shipping routes. Given supplies $s_i\ge 0$, demands $d_j\ge 0$, and constant per-unit costs $c_{ij}$ for $(i,j)\in A$, with $\sum_{i\in I}s_i=\sum_{j\in J}d_j$, the classical transportation problem is
\[
\min_{x\ge 0}\ \sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=s_i\ \ (i\in I),\qquad
\sum_{i:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=d_j\ \ (j\in J).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical balanced transportation problem chooses nonnegative direct shipments along available source-to-destination routes. Every source stockpile must be exhausted, every destination demand fulfilled, and total linear shipping cost minimized. Exact fulfillment implies equality of total supply and total demand.
assumptions_latex: I,J\text{ are the source and destination index sets}
A\subseteq I\times J\text{ is the set of available direct shipping routes}
s_i\ge 0\ (i\in I),\quad d_j\ge 0\ (j\in J)
\sum_{i\in I}s_i=\sum_{j\in J}d_j
c_{ij}\text{ is a constant per-unit shipping cost for each }(i,j)\in A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x_{ij}\ge 0}\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=s_i\ \forall i,\ \sum_{i:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=d_j\ \forall j\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Finite Optimal Transportation Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and finiteness of the optimum for the complete balanced transportation LP.

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced Transportation Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear programming formulation and coefficient structure of the balanced, uncapacitated transportation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given supplies \(a_i\ge 0\), demands \(b_j\ge 0\), and route costs \(c_{ij}\), with \(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\), the balanced transportation problem is
\[
\min_{x_{ij}\ge 0}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=a_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ij}=b_j\ (j=1,\ldots,n).
\]
When variables are grouped by origin, the constraint matrix has block form
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf 1^T&&&\\
&\mathbf 1^T&&\\
&&\ddots&\\
&&&\mathbf 1^T\\
I&I&\cdots&I
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced transportation problem minimizes total shipping cost over nonnegative shipments whose row sums equal supplies and whose column sums equal demands, under equality of total supply and total demand. Its constraint matrix has the standard bipartite block structure.
assumptions_latex: m,n\in\mathbb N
a_i\ge 0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
b_j\ge 0\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=\sum_{j=1}^n b_j
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\ge 0}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=a_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_{ij}=b_j\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical transportation LP and balancing conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced complete-route transportation formulation, the excess-supply dummy-destination reduction, and the limited large-cost convention for discouraged or prohibited routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, $s_i,d_j>0$, and $c_{ij}\in\mathbb R$. If $\sum_{i=1}^m s_i=\sum_{j=1}^n d_j$, the balanced transportation problem is
\[
\min_{x\ge0}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=s_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ij}=d_j\ (j=1,\ldots,n).
\]
On the complete bipartite origin-destination graph, define $b=(s_1,\ldots,s_m,-d_1,\ldots,-d_n)^T$ and $a_{ij}=e_i-e_{m+j}$. Then the formulation is $\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}$. If $\sum_i s_i>\sum_j d_j$, adding a dummy destination with $d_{n+1}=\sum_i s_i-\sum_jd_j$ and $c_{i,n+1}=0$ balances the instance. A prohibited connection may be retained in the complete-route formulation with a sufficiently large cost so that its variable is discouraged as an artificial variable; this convention is not, without a quantified valid cost bound, the same as imposing $x_{ij}=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced transportation problem is a minimum-cost nonnegative-flow LP whose row totals equal supplies and column totals equal demands. Its matrix is the node-arc incidence matrix of a complete bipartite graph. Excess supply can be absorbed by a zero-cost dummy destination. The extract also gives a large-route-cost convention for prohibited connections, but that convention should not be stated as an unconditional hard prohibition.
assumptions_latex: m,n\in\mathbb N
s_i>0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
d_j>0\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\quad(i=1,\ldots,m;\ j=1,\ldots,n)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\sum_i s_i=\sum_j d_j\right)\Longrightarrow P=\left\{x\ge0:\sum_jx_{ij}=s_i,\ \sum_ix_{ij}=d_j\right\}=\{x\ge0:Ax=b\},\quad a_{ij}=e_i-e_{m+j};\qquad \sum_i s_i>\sum_jd_j\Longrightarrow d_{n+1}=\sum_i s_i-\sum_jd_j,\ c_{i,n+1}=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility, boundedness, and attainment for balanced transportation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive feasibility, coordinate bounds for every feasible shipment, and consequent attainment of any finite linear-cost objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let $s_i,d_j>0$, and suppose
\[
d=\sum_{i=1}^m s_i=\sum_{j=1}^n d_j.
\]
For the complete-route balanced transportation constraints,
\[
x_{ij}=\frac{s_id_j}{d}\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m;\ j=1,\ldots,n)
\]
is feasible. Every feasible $x$ satisfies
\[
0\le x_{ij}\le\min\{s_i,d_j\}.
\]
Hence the feasible region is nonempty and bounded. Consequently, for any finite real cost vector $c$, the transportation linear program attains an optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive supplies and demands having the same total, the product shipment $s_i d_j/d$ is feasible. Every feasible route flow is at most both its origin supply and destination demand, so the feasible region is nonempty and bounded. Therefore every finite linear-cost objective attains a minimum on it.
assumptions_latex: m,n\in\mathbb N
s_i>0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
d_j>0\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
d=\sum_{i=1}^m s_i=\sum_{j=1}^n d_j
c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\quad(i=1,\ldots,m;\ j=1,\ldots,n)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{ij}=\frac{s_id_j}{d}\text{ is feasible},\qquad 0\le x_{ij}\le\min\{s_i,d_j\}\text{ for every feasible }x,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^Tx\ne\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbalanced Transportation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transportation regimes whose aggregate supply and demand differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unbalanced transportation model has total supply \(S=\sum_{i\in I}s_i\) and total demand \(D=\sum_{j\in J}d_j\) with \(S\ne D\). The equality-form constraints requiring all supply to be shipped and all demand to be met are then infeasible, because summing them would require \(S=D\). If \(S>D\), a feasible complete-bipartite inequality model may impose \(\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i\) and \(\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j\); if \(S<D\), it may impose \(\sum_jx_{ij}=s_i\) and \(\sum_ix_{ij}\le d_j\). Penalties or dummy nodes can account for the unmatched quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When total supply and demand differ, the all-equalities model is infeasible. Inequalities, penalties, or a dummy node must represent the unmatched amount.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite nonempty sets.
Every pair \((i,j)\in I\times J\) is an allowed shipment arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\ne D\) excludes feasibility of simultaneously enforcing \(\sum_jx_{ij}=s_i\) and \(\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j\).

notation.meaning: shipment from origin i to destination j

knowledge_statements.title: Dummy-Node Balancing Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-cost dummy-node completion of an unbalanced transportation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let supplies and demands satisfy \(a_i,b_j\ge 0\). If \(\sum_i a_i>\sum_j b_j\), adjoin a dummy destination \(j_0\) with demand \(b_{j_0}=\sum_i a_i-\sum_j b_j\); if the inequality is reversed, adjoin a dummy source analogously. Assign zero cost to every dummy arc. The augmented model is balanced. Restriction to original arcs maps each augmented feasible flow to a flow satisfying all original equalities on the smaller-total side and inequalities on the larger-total side; dummy flows equal the unused surplus. Conversely, every such unbalanced flow extends to an augmented balanced flow, with unchanged objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a zero-cost dummy destination or source whose demand or supply equals the imbalance. Dummy flow records unused capacity, and original objective values are preserved.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.
The unbalanced model permits unused quantity on the side having the larger total.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{unbalanced feasible flows}\longleftrightarrow\text{balanced augmented feasible flows}\), with equal original and augmented costs.

notation.meaning: dummy destination when total supply exceeds total demand

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Capacitated Transportation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced transportation polytope with individual upper bounds on routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite source and destination sets \(I,J\), supplies \(a_i\ge 0\), demands \(b_j\ge 0\), arc costs \(c_{ij}\), and capacities \(u_{ij}\ge 0\), the arc-capacitated transportation LP is
\[\min_x\ \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=a_i,\quad \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=b_j,\quad 0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Forbidden-Route Transportation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transportation over a prescribed bipartite route graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\subseteq I\times J\) be the permitted routes. Forbidden-route transportation is represented either by retaining variables only for \((i,j)\in E\), or equivalently by imposing \(x_{ij}=0\) for \((i,j)\notin E\). Its feasible set is
\[P_E=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:\ \sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}=a_i\ \forall i,\quad \sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}=b_j\ \forall j\right\}.\]
Thus feasibility requires more than equality of total supply and demand; the permitted bipartite graph must support the prescribed node balances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Remove every forbidden route, or fix its flow to zero. Feasibility then depends on whether the remaining bipartite graph can carry all supplies and demands.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bounded Transportation Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of route lower bounds by an affine flow shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider route bounds \(x_{ij}\ge \ell_{ij}\ge 0\). Define \(y_{ij}=x_{ij}-\ell_{ij}\), residual supplies \(a'_i=a_i-\sum_j\ell_{ij}\), and residual demands \(b'_j=b_j-\sum_i\ell_{ij}\). Then \(x\) satisfies the original transportation equalities and lower bounds exactly when \(y\ge 0\) satisfies
\[\sum_jy_{ij}=a'_i,\qquad \sum_iy_{ij}=b'_j.\]
Hence feasibility requires \(a'_i,b'_j\ge 0\) and feasibility of the residual transportation problem. For linear costs, \(\sum_{ij}c_{ij}x_{ij}=\sum_{ij}c_{ij}y_{ij}+\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\ell_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract each route's lower bound. The remaining variables solve a transportation problem with residual supplies and demands, while the objective changes by a constant.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.
\(\ell_{ij}\ge 0\) is specified on every modeled route.
Original supplies and demands are balanced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible}\iff y=x-\ell\text{ is feasible for residual balances }(a',b')\).

children.title: Classical Transportation Structure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Restrictions that weaken or destroy the standard transportation formulation structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Transportation Structure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between bipartite network structure and arbitrary side-constrained LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Route deletion and finite lower or upper bounds retain a bipartite network-flow formulation after standard variable shifts and residual-capacity transformations. Arbitrary constraints coupling unrelated arcs need not retain the transportation matrix or its integrality. For example, the \(2\times2\) assignment polytope has points
\[x(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t&1-t\\1-t&t\end{pmatrix},\qquad 0\le t\le1.\]
Adding the side constraint \(x_{11}\le \tfrac12\) creates the extreme point \(x(1/2)\), which is fractional. Thus balanced row and column equations alone do not protect classical transportation integrality after a nonnetwork side constraint is introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route bounds preserve network structure, but arbitrary cross-route constraints may destroy it. A two-by-two assignment example gains a fractional extreme point after one side constraint.
assumptions_latex: The base model has balanced bipartite node-balance equations.
Additional restrictions may couple multiple route variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{11}\le \tfrac12\) makes \(x(1/2)\) a fractional extreme point of the restricted \(2\times2\) assignment polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation Basis Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spanning-tree characterization for balanced transportation bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a balanced \(m\)-source, \(n\)-destination transportation polytope on the complete bipartite graph, the row and column equations have rank \(m+n-1\). A set of \(m+n-1\) route columns is a basis exactly when its bipartite edges form a spanning tree. Consequently, every basic feasible solution has at most \(m+n-1\) positive entries. It is nondegenerate exactly when all basic flows are positive; in a degenerate basic feasible solution, a spanning-tree basis may contain zero-flow basic arcs, while the positive-flow support is a forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transportation bases are bipartite spanning trees. Nondegenerate bases have positive flow on every tree edge; degeneracy occurs when some basic tree edges carry zero flow.
assumptions_latex: The route graph is the complete bipartite graph \(K_{m,n}\).
Supplies and demands are balanced and the feasible set is nonempty.
One redundant balance equation is omitted when forming a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is a basis}\iff (I\cup J,B)\text{ is a spanning tree of }K_{m,n}\), and \(|B|=m+n-1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessary Subset-Balance Condition for Transportation Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transportation-specific necessary condition for a degenerate spanning-tree basis, with its nondegeneracy and no-cycling consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be a basic feasible solution of a transportation problem, with row set \(M\), column set \(N\), supplies \(s_i\), demands \(d_j\), and a spanning-tree basis graph. If \(x\) is degenerate, then deleting a zero-valued basic edge separates the basis tree and yields nonempty proper index sets \(I\subsetneq M\) and \(J\subsetneq N\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in I}s_i=\sum_{j\in J}d_j.
\]
Consequently, if no such pair \((I,J)\) satisfies this equality, transportation bases are nondegenerate and the transportation algorithm cannot cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate transportation basis implies that some nonempty proper collection of rows and some nonempty proper collection of columns have equal total supply and demand. If no such equality exists, transportation bases are nondegenerate and cycling cannot occur.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a basic feasible solution of the standard transportation constraints with row set \(M\), column set \(N\), supplies \(s_i\), and demands \(d_j\).
The basic cells form a spanning tree of the bipartite row-column graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
x	ext{ degenerate}\Rightarrow\exists\,\varnothing
e I\subsetneq M,\ \varnothing
e J\subsetneq N:\ \sum_{i\in I}s_i=\sum_{j\in J}d_j;\qquad \left[
exists(I,J)	ext{ satisfying this equality}ight]\Rightarrow	ext{nondegeneracy and no cycling}.

knowledge_statements.title: Square Assignment Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced one-to-one assignment and its LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For two sets \(I,J\) with \(|I|=|J|=n\), the square assignment LP is
\[\min_x\ \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\quad \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\ \forall j,\quad x_{ij}\ge0.\]
Its feasible region is the doubly stochastic polytope. Its extreme points are permutation matrices, so an optimal extreme point gives a one-to-one assignment whenever the LP is feasible and bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square assignment matches two equally sized sets one-to-one. Its LP relaxation is doubly stochastic and has permutation matrices as extreme points.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite with \(|I|=|J|=n\).
Every pair \((i,j)\) is an available assignment.
Costs \(c_{ij}\) are finite real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x\ge0:x\mathbf1=\mathbf1,\ x^{\mathsf T}\mathbf1=\mathbf1\}\), and every extreme point of \(P\) is a permutation matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness of the Square Assignment LP Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States equality of the integer-assignment and nonnegative-LP optimal values and existence of an integral LP optimum; it does not claim that every LP optimum is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\). For the square assignment model, replacing \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) by \(x_{ij}\ge 0\), while retaining \(\sum_jx_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\), \(\sum_ix_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\), and the objective \(\min\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\), preserves the optimal value. Moreover, the relaxed linear program has an optimal permutation matrix, although it may also have fractional optimal solutions.

At least one optimal solution of the resulting linear program is a permutation matrix, though fractional optima may coexist when the optimum is not unique.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Injective assignment from the smaller side into the larger side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I,J\) be finite with \(|I|=m\le n=|J|\). The rectangular assignment polytope that assigns every member of \(I\) to a distinct member of \(J\) is
\[P=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_+^{I\times J}:\ \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\quad \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}\le1\ \forall j\right\}.\]
With objective \(\min\sum_{ij}c_{ij}x_{ij}\), its integral feasible points encode injections from \(I\) into \(J\); the displayed LP has integral extreme points because it is a bipartite matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every member of the smaller set is assigned once, while each member of the larger set is used at most once. Integral solutions encode injections.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite with \(|I|\le|J|\).
All displayed pairs are admissible assignments.
Costs are linear in assignment variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x\ge0:\sum_jx_{ij}=1,\ \sum_ix_{ij}\le1\}\), and the extreme points of \(P\) are integral.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-\(k\) bipartite partial-assignment formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite sets \(I,J\) and an integer \(0\le k\le\min\{|I|,|J|\}\), the cardinality-\(k\) partial-assignment polytope is
\[P_k=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_+^{I\times J}:\ \sum_jx_{ij}\le1\ \forall i,\quad \sum_ix_{ij}\le1\ \forall j,\quad \sum_{i,j}x_{ij}=k\right\}.\]
Its integral points are matchings containing exactly \(k\) pairs. The constraint matrix admits integral extreme points, so optimizing a linear cost over \(P_k\) yields an integral optimal extreme point whenever \(P_k\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cardinality-k partial assignment selects exactly k disjoint agent-task pairs. Neither side must be completely assigned, and the LP has integral extreme points.

\(k\) is an integer satisfying \(0\le k\le\min\{|I|,|J|\}\).
All displayed pairs are admissible.

knowledge_statements.title: Dummy-Vertex Square Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square completion of rectangular assignment by zero-cost dummy vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(|I|=m<n=|J|\) in a rectangular assignment requiring every \(i\in I\) to be matched. Add a dummy set \(D\) with \(|D|=n-m\) to the smaller side and give every dummy edge cost zero. The resulting instance on \(I\cup D\) and \(J\) is square. Restricting any square perfect assignment to \(I\times J\) gives a rectangular assignment, and every rectangular assignment extends by matching its \(n-m\) unused vertices of \(J\) to dummy vertices. Corresponding solutions have equal objective values, although extensions differ by permutations of dummy vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pad the smaller side with zero-cost dummy vertices. Perfect square assignments then correspond to rectangular assignments, apart from irrelevant permutations among dummy vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(I,J\) are finite with \(|I|=m<n=|J|\).
Every original member of \(I\) must be assigned once.
Dummy edges are all available and have zero cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Optional-Matching Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite matching in which vertices may remain unmatched.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite vertex sets \(I,J\), admissible edges \(E\subseteq I\times J\), and edge rewards \(w_{ij}\in\mathbb R\), the optional-matching LP is
\[\max_x\ \sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}\le1\ \forall i,\quad \sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}\le1\ \forall j,\quad x\ge0.\]
No cardinality equality is imposed, so the empty matching is feasible. Extreme points are incidence vectors of matchings; negative-reward edges can therefore be omitted without forcing replacement assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optional matching permits every vertex to remain unmatched. The empty matching is feasible, and integral extreme points select disjoint rewarded edges.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.
\(E\subseteq I\times J\) is the admissible edge set.
Rewards \(w_{ij}\) are finite real numbers.

children.title: Capacitated Assignment

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized assignment LP with item-dependent resource consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For items \(I\), bins \(J\), assignment costs \(c_{ij}\), resource consumptions \(d_{ij}\ge0\), and bin capacities \(b_j\ge0\), the capacitated assignment relaxation is
\[\min_x\ \sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\quad \sum_{i\in I}d_{ij}x_{ij}\le b_j\ \forall j,\quad 0\le x_{ij}\le1.\]
Requiring \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) gives the generalized capacitated assignment problem. When consumptions vary by item and bin, the LP matrix is not generally a bipartite incidence matrix and fractional extreme points may occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each item chooses one bin, while item-dependent resource use must fit bin capacities. The natural LP relaxation need not retain classical assignment integrality.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.
Every item has at least one admissible bin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x\in[0,1]^{I\times J}:\sum_jx_{ij}=1,\ \sum_id_{ij}x_{ij}\le b_j\}\), which need not be integral.

children.title: Side-Constrained Assignment

knowledge_statements.title: Side-Constrained Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single valid side inequality can destroy integrality of the assignment relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_2=\{X\in\mathbb R_+^{2\times2}:X\mathbf1=\mathbf1,\ X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf1=\mathbf1\}\). Every \(X\in B_2\) has the form \(X(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t&1-t\\1-t&t\end{pmatrix}\) with \(0\le t\le1\). Adding the side constraint \(x_{11}\le\tfrac12\) produces the polytope \(B_2\cap\{X:x_{11}\le\tfrac12\}\), whose endpoint \(X(\tfrac12)\) is a fractional vertex. Thus an additional linear constraint need not preserve the permutation-vertex property, even when its coefficients and right-hand side are rational.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the constraint x11 ≤ 1/2 to the 2-by-2 assignment polytope creates a fractional vertex, so arbitrary side constraints do not preserve assignment integrality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb R_+^{2\times2}\)
\(X\mathbf1=X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf1=\mathbf1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X(\tfrac12)\) is a fractional vertex of the side-constrained polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Index Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-index axial assignment already lies outside the classical bipartite integrality regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n=2\), consider \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^{2\times2\times2}:\sum_{j,k}x_{ijk}=1,\ \sum_{i,k}x_{ijk}=1,\ \sum_{i,j}x_{ijk}=1\}\). The tensor with \(x_{111}=x_{122}=x_{212}=x_{221}=\tfrac12\) and all other entries zero is feasible and fractional. No integral feasible tensor has support contained in these four positions, because selecting any one of them leaves no supported position using all complementary indices. Consequently this point is not a convex combination of integral feasible tensors, and \(P\) is not integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The 2-by-2-by-2 axial assignment relaxation contains a fractional point outside the convex hull of integral assignments; classical two-index exactness therefore fails.
assumptions_latex: Each one-index marginal equals \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\ne\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\{0,1\}^{2\times2\times2})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Assignment Integrality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the structural assumptions supporting classical assignment LP exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(U,V,E)\) be bipartite and let \(b\in\mathbb Z^{U\cup V}\). The polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:Ax=b\}\), where \(A\) is the node-edge incidence matrix, has integral vertices whenever it is nonempty. This conclusion follows from bipartite incidence and integral right-hand sides. It is not guaranteed after replacing bipartite incidence by a nonbipartite matching matrix, adjoining arbitrary side inequalities, or introducing three-index marginal constraints; each modification can admit fractional extreme points or fractional feasible points outside the integral hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipartite incidence with integral balances guarantees integral assignment vertices; nonbipartite, side-constrained, and higher-index variants can lose that guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(U,V,E)\) is bipartite.
\(b\in\mathbb Z^{U\cup V}\).
\(P\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every vertex of \(P\) is integral; the stated structural extensions need not retain this property.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical assignment LP and its integral matching interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The square minimum-cost assignment formulation, exactness of its LP relaxation, and its zero-one-cost bipartite-matching specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), the assignment problem is \(\min \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}f_{ij}\) subject to \(\sum_i f_{ij}=1\;(j=1,\ldots,n)\), \(\sum_j f_{ij}=1\;(i=1,\ldots,n)\), and \(f_{ij}\ge 0\). These constraints imply \(f_{ij}\le 1\), and the problem has an optimal solution in \(\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\). If \(c_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) and \(c_{ij}=0\) exactly for compatible pairs, minimizing the objective maximizes the number of compatible assigned pairs; the optimum is zero exactly when a perfect matching exists, and compatible matching can also be formulated as a maximum-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical square assignment problem is an LP with one unit assigned to every person and every project. Its upper bounds are redundant, and it has a zero-one optimal solution, so the LP relaxation is exact. With zero-one costs indicating incompatibility, it becomes bipartite matching: the objective maximizes compatible pairs, has value zero exactly for a perfect matching, and admits a maximum-flow formulation.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb N
C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}
f\in\mathbb R_+^{n\times n}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f^*\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\text{ optimal};\qquad c_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\Longrightarrow \operatorname{val}=0\iff\text{a perfect compatible matching exists}.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Matching Matrix Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence representation underlying total unimodularity of bipartite assignment constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bipartite graph \(G=(U,V,E)\), define \(A\in\{0,1\}^{(U\cup V)\times E}\) by \(A_{we}=1\) exactly when vertex \(w\) is incident to edge \(e\). Multiplying every row indexed by \(V\) by \(-1\) converts \(A\) into an oriented node-arc incidence matrix. Hence \(A\) is totally unimodular. Therefore, for every integral vector \(b\), every vertex of \(\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:Ax=b\}\) is integral whenever the polyhedron is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signing one bipartition converts the matching matrix into an oriented incidence matrix, proving total unimodularity and integral vertices for integral balances.

\(b\in\mathbb Z^{U\cup V}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Doubly Stochastic Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the square assignment relaxation and its integral permutation points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(n\ge1\), the doubly stochastic polytope is \[B_n=\left\{X=(x_{ij})\in\mathbb R_+^{n\times n}:\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1\ \text{for every }i,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\ \text{for every }j\right\}.\] Its zero-one members are exactly the permutation matrices: each such matrix has precisely one entry equal to \(1\) in every row and every column. Thus \(B_n\) is the standard linear relaxation of the perfect assignment set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The doubly stochastic polytope consists of nonnegative square matrices whose row and column sums are one; its zero-one points are permutation matrices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_n\cap\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) is the set of \(n\)-by-\(n\) permutation matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-Vertex Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Birkhoff polytope vertex characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(n\ge1\), a matrix \(X\in B_n\) is an extreme point of \(B_n\) if and only if \(X\) is a permutation matrix. Consequently, for every cost matrix \(C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), the linear program \(\min\{\langle C,X\rangle:X\in B_n\}\) has an optimal permutation matrix. Hence the classical square assignment LP relaxation has the same optimal value as its zero-one formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vertices of the doubly stochastic polytope are exactly permutation matrices, so linear assignment optimization always has an integral optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Doubly Stochastic Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex decomposition form of the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(X\in B_n\), there exist permutation matrices \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge0\) such that \[X=\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_kP_k,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_k=1.\] The decomposition may be chosen with \(m\le(n-1)^2+1\). Conversely, every such convex combination belongs to \(B_n\). Therefore \(B_n\) equals the convex hull of the permutation matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every doubly stochastic matrix is a convex combination of permutation matrices, with at most (n−1)²+1 terms needed.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge1\) is an integer.
\(X\in B_n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Exactness Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates classical bipartite exactness from three common nonclassical extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Classical assignment exactness relies on a bipartite node-edge incidence system with integral balances. Three changes fall outside that guarantee: nonbipartite degree constraints may have half-integral odd-cycle solutions; intersecting a doubly stochastic polytope with an additional linear inequality may create fractional vertices; and three-index one-marginal constraints may admit fractional points outside the convex hull of integral assignments. Thus row-column balance alone does not imply LP exactness once the bipartite two-index incidence structure is lost or altered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd cycles, arbitrary side constraints, and higher-index marginals can produce fractional assignment relaxations beyond the classical bipartite regime.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation modifies or leaves the bipartite two-index incidence regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The modified assignment relaxation need not equal the convex hull of its integral feasible assignments.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three named failure regimes fit the container, but the record provides neither formal counterexamples nor an inspectable source supporting the aggregated boundary claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation Simplex Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-simplex specialization using spanning-tree bases of a finite balanced transportation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite nonempty index sets. Given supplies \(a_i\ge0\) for \(i\in I\), demands \(b_j\ge0\) for \(j\in J\), costs \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\), and \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\), consider variables \(x_{ij}\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=a_i\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=b_j\). Initialize a feasible basic plan whose basic arcs form a spanning tree of the complete bipartite graph on \(I\cup J\), allowing zero-valued basic arcs under degeneracy. Compute potentials satisfying \(u_i+v_j=c_{ij}\) on basic arcs. If every reduced cost \(c_{ij}-u_i-v_j\ge0\), output the plan. Otherwise choose an arc with negative reduced cost according to a finite anti-cycling rule, insert it, adjust flows around the resulting unique alternating cycle by the largest feasible amount, delete a blocking basic arc according to that rule, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite balanced transportation problem, transportation simplex pivots between bipartite spanning-tree bases using reduced costs and alternating-cycle flow adjustments until all reduced costs are nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite and nonempty.
\(a_i,b_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\).
A feasible basic transportation plan is available.
A finite anti-cycling pivot rule is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon termination, the output minimizes \(\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) over all feasible transportation plans.

notation.meaning: Finite supply-node and demand-node index sets.
Flow transported from supply node i to demand node j.

For each nonbasic cell, compute \(z_{ij}-c_{ij}\); stop when the optimality test is satisfied, or otherwise select an entering cell. Determine a leaving basic cell, construct the resulting basic feasible solution, and repeat the reduced-cost step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find an initial basic feasible transportation solution, compute the reduced-cost quantities, stop if the optimality test holds, or choose entering and leaving cells, update the basis, and repeat.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a transportation linear program represented by a transportation tableau.
The primal simplex method is applied using transportation basic solutions and pivots.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These initialization, reduced-cost, entering-cell, leaving-cell, and basis-update operations form the transportation-tableau specialization of a primal-simplex iteration.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transportation Cycle Pivot and Leaving-Cell Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-ratio and alternating-cycle update after selection of an entering transportation cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((k,\ell)\) be an entering nonbasic cell and let \(\mathbf y_{k\ell}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{m+n-1}\) be its representation in the current transportation basis. If \(\widehat x_{ij}\) is the current value of basic cell \((i,j)\), set \[\Delta=\min\{\widehat x_{ij}:(i,j)\in B,\ (\mathbf y_{k\ell})_{ij}=+1\}.\] Increase \(x_{k\ell}\) by \(\Delta\); decrease by \(\Delta\) every basic cycle variable whose representation coefficient is \(+1\); increase by \(\Delta\) every basic cycle variable whose coefficient is \(-1\); and leave all other variables unchanged. At least one minimizing basic variable reaches zero. Choose one such cell to leave the basis and include \((k,\ell)\) as basic; ties may leave additional zero-valued basic variables and hence a degenerate solution. The signed cycle update preserves all transportation row and column balances and nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After choosing an entering cell, use its unique alternating cycle. The step is the smallest value among cycle cells that must decrease. Apply the alternating plus-minus update, choose a minimizing zero cell to leave, and include the entering cell; feasibility is preserved, with ties potentially causing degeneracy.
assumptions_latex: The current transportation solution is basic and feasible.
A nonbasic entering cell \((k,\ell)\) has been selected.
Adding \((k,\ell)\) to the basic tree determines a unique alternating cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta=\min\{\widehat x_{ij}:(i,j)\in B,\ (\mathbf y_{k\ell})_{ij}=+1\},\quad\text{and the signed cycle update preserves feasibility while making every minimizer leaving-eligible.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Northwest Corner Rule and Basic-Feasibility Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transportation-simplex initialization for a balanced, unrestricted transportation tableau, including the zero-basic-variable convention for degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an \(m\times n\) transportation problem with \(s_i\ge0\), \(d_j\ge0\), and \(\sum_i s_i=\sum_j d_j\), initialize \(\widehat s_i=s_i\) and \(\widehat d_j=d_j\). Starting at \((1,1)\), assign \(x_{k\ell}=\min\{\widehat s_k,\widehat d_\ell\}\), subtract this value from both residuals, and move right if residual supply remains or down if the row is exhausted. When a row and column are exhausted simultaneously before completion, retain an eligible adjacent cell as basic at value zero and advance only one index. Continuing to \((m,n)\) produces \(m+n-1\) nonnegative basic variables, counting zero-valued basic variables. The graph of basic cells is connected, spanning, and acyclic, so the resulting allocation is a basic feasible transportation solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a balanced unrestricted transportation tableau, allocate the smaller residual supply or demand at the current northwest cell, update both residuals, and move right or down. When both residuals vanish together, retain a suitable zero-valued basic cell to represent degeneracy. The resulting m+n−1 basic cells form a spanning tree and define a basic feasible solution.
assumptions_latex: s_i\ge0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad d_j\ge0\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}d_j
All cells of the \(m\times n\) transportation tableau are admissible.
Zero-valued basic cells are retained when simultaneous row and column exhaustion would otherwise reduce the basis count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The northwest corner rule produces a basic feasible transportation solution whose basic-cell graph is a spanning tree with \(m+n-1\) cells.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transportation Reduced-Cost Computation and Optimality Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle and node-potential computations under the source convention \(z_{ij}-c_{ij}\) for a minimization transportation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a feasible transportation basis whose basic-cell graph is a spanning tree. For a nonbasic cell \((i,j)\), \[z_{ij}-c_{ij}=\mathbf c_B\mathbf B^{-1}\mathbf a_{ij}-c_{ij}=\mathbf c_B\mathbf y_{ij}-c_{ij},\] where \(\mathbf y_{ij}\) has alternating \(1\) and \(-1\) coefficients on the unique cycle created by adding \((i,j)\) to the basic tree. Equivalently, determine potentials \(u_p,v_q\) satisfying \(u_p-v_q=c_{pq}\) on every basic cell and fix one potential to remove additive indeterminacy. Then \[z_{ij}-c_{ij}=u_i-v_j-c_{ij}.\] Under this sign convention, the feasible basis is optimal if and only if \(z_{ij}-c_{ij}\le0\) for every nonbasic cell; any cell with \(z_{ij}-c_{ij}>0\) is eligible to enter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a transportation basis, compute each nonbasic cell's reduced-cost quantity either by alternating basic costs around its unique induced cycle or by solving for row and column potentials on the basic tree. With the source's sign convention, the basis is optimal exactly when every such quantity is nonpositive, while a positive quantity identifies an eligible entering cell.
assumptions_latex: The transportation problem is a minimization problem in the source's tableau convention.
The current transportation solution is basic and feasible.
The basic-cell graph is a spanning tree.
u_p-v_q=c_{pq}\quad\text{for every basic cell }(p,q),\text{ with one potential fixed.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_{ij}-c_{ij}=u_i-v_j-c_{ij},\qquad \left(\forall(i,j)\notin B:\ z_{ij}-c_{ij}\le0\right)\iff B\text{ is optimal},\qquad z_{k\ell}-c_{k\ell}>0\Rightarrow(k,\ell)\text{ is entering-eligible}.

knowledge_statements.title: Hungarian Primal–Dual Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal–dual augmentation for the square minimum-cost assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For costs \(c_{ij}\), maintain dual labels \(u_i,v_j\) satisfying \(u_i+v_j\le c_{ij}\) and a matching using only equality edges \(E_0=\{(i,j):u_i+v_j=c_{ij}\}\). Initialize any feasible labels and an empty equality-edge matching. Repeatedly grow an alternating forest from an unmatched row. If it reaches an unmatched column, augment. Otherwise let \(S,T\) be the reached rows and columns, set \(\delta=\min_{i\in S,j\notin T}(c_{ij}-u_i-v_j)\), increase \(u_i\) on \(S\), decrease \(v_j\) on \(T\), and continue. Output the matching when it is perfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hungarian method maintains feasible prices and augments along zero-reduced-cost edges, updating labels when the equality graph lacks an augmenting path.
assumptions_latex: \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) for \(1\le i,j\le n\).
The complete bipartite assignment problem is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The final perfect matching and labels satisfy complementary slackness and are primal-dual optimal.

notation.meaning: Dual labels for rows and columns.
The equality graph of zero reduced-cost edges.
Vertex sets reached by the alternating forest.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal–dual Hungarian procedure is coherently stated and algorithm-kind fits the method-family leaf, but its correctness and termination claims lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Auction Price-Adjustment Family
children.top_down_role: Assignment methods organized around competitive bidding and evolving prices.

knowledge_statements.title: Auction Price-Adjustment Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epsilon-relaxed price adjustment for maximum-benefit square assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), let \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) be the benefit of assigning bidder \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) to object \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Initialize prices \(p_j=0\) and leave every bidder unassigned. Repeatedly choose an unassigned bidder \(i\). Let \(j^*\) maximize \(a_{ij}-p_j\), let \(w_i\) be the second-largest value among \(\{a_{ij}-p_j:1\le j\le n\}\), and set \(p_{j^*}\leftarrow p_{j^*}+a_{ij^*}-p_{j^*}-w_i+\varepsilon\). Assign \(i\) to \(j^*\), unassigning its previous owner if necessary. Stop when every bidder is assigned, and denote the resulting permutation by \(\sigma\). The output satisfies \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness and has total benefit within \(n\varepsilon\) of optimum. If all \(a_{ij}\) are integers and \(n\varepsilon<1\), then \(\sigma\) is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a square assignment problem with at least two bidders, auction repeatedly lets an unassigned bidder raise the price of its best object. The resulting permutation is within n epsilon of optimal and is exact for integral benefits when n epsilon is less than one.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge2\) is an integer.
\(a_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) for \(1\le i,j\le n\).
\(\varepsilon>0\).
For the exactness conclusion, \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\) and \(n\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{OPT}-\sum_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)}\le n\varepsilon\); under integral benefits and \(n\varepsilon<1\), \(\sigma\) is optimal.

notation.meaning: The second-largest net benefit available to bidder i.
The positive auction increment and complementary-slackness tolerance.
The permutation representing the final assignment.

children.title: Alternating-Structure Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparison of augmenting structures used across the two method families.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Structure Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares the alternating structures and dual conditions used by Hungarian and auction methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For square assignment, both method families maintain a partial matching and object-side prices derived from the assignment dual. The Hungarian family preserves exact dual feasibility and searches an alternating forest in the zero-reduced-cost equality graph, changing labels only when no augmenting equality path exists. The auction family performs a one-bidder alternating displacement chain and maintains \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness rather than exact equality. Thus both exploit alternating reassignment, but Hungarian augmentation is equality-graph global whereas an auction bid is locally price-driven.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both methods use alternating reassignment and dual prices; Hungarian searches exact equality graphs, while auction uses local displacement under epsilon-complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a feasible square assignment instance.
Hungarian labels are dual feasible.
Auction prices satisfy the chosen \(\varepsilon\)-scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hungarian updates preserve exact dual feasibility, whereas auction updates preserve \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness; both terminate with primal-dual optimality under their stated exactness conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison appropriately distinguishes equality-graph augmentation from epsilon-relaxed local displacement, but the comparative and termination claims have no inspectable citations.

children.title: Assignment Price-System Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exact, scaled, or approximate price organizations for assignment optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Price-System Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and approximate price systems for the minimum-cost square assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let costs be \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) for \(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The assignment LP minimizes \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) subject to \(\sum_jx_{ij}=1\), \(\sum_ix_{ij}=1\), and \(x_{ij}\ge 0\). Its price system consists of \(u_i,v_j\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \(u_i+v_j\le c_{ij}\), and its dual objective is \(\sum_i u_i+\sum_jv_j\). A permutation \(\pi\) and feasible prices are jointly optimal exactly when \(u_i+v_{\pi(i)}=c_{i,\pi(i)}\) for every \(i\). Under \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness, these equalities are relaxed to \(c_{i,\pi(i)}-\varepsilon\le u_i+v_{\pi(i)}\le c_{i,\pi(i)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible vertex prices lower-bound assignment costs; equality on every assigned edge certifies optimality, while epsilon equality defines an approximate price regime.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\) and the complete bipartite assignment problem has finite real costs.
\(\pi\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\) is optimal when \(u_i+v_j\le c_{ij}\) for all \(i,j\) and \(u_i+v_{\pi(i)}=c_{i,\pi(i)}\) for all \(i\).

notation.meaning: cost of assigning agent i to object j
dual prices on the two bipartition classes

children.title: Assignment Through Minimum-Cost Flow
children.top_down_role: The structural route from assignment models to successive shortest-path and network-flow methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Through Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of a balanced bipartite assignment instance to a unit-capacity minimum-cost flow instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given bipartition classes \(U,V\) with \(|U|=|V|=n\) and edge costs \(c_{ij}\), construct a network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), arcs \((s,i)\) for \(i\in U\), arcs \((i,j)\) for admissible \((i,j)\in U\times V\), and arcs \((j,t)\) for \(j\in V\). Give every arc capacity one, assign cost \(c_{ij}\) only to \((i,j)\), and require an \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(n\). Integral feasible flows correspond bijectively to perfect assignments through \(x_{ij}=f_{ij}\), preserving objective value. Thus minimum-cost assignment is a unit-capacity minimum-cost flow problem and may be solved by applicable successive shortest-path methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfect assignment is exactly an integral value-n flow in a three-layer unit-capacity network, with identical cost.
assumptions_latex: \(|U|=|V|=n\) and a perfect assignment exists.
All assignment costs \(c_{ij}\) are finite on admissible edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{\text{assignments}}\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}=\min_{f:\,|f|=n}\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}f_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: assignment indicator corresponding to the middle-layer flow

children.title: Total Unimodularity
children.top_down_role: The central matrix-structural route from linear descriptions to integral polyhedra.

children.title: Total-Unimodularity Recognition Calculus
children.top_down_role: Classical viewpoints for recognizing and building totally unimodular matrices.

children.title: Subdeterminant Viewpoint
children.top_down_role: The determinant-based organization of total unimodularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Subdeterminant Viewpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Determinantal definition of total unimodularity for finite real matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular if every square submatrix \(B=A[I,J]\), where \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(|I|=|J|\), satisfies \(\det(B)\in\{-1,0,1\}\). Equivalently, every square subdeterminant of \(A\) has absolute value at most one and is integral. In particular, the one-by-one subdeterminants imply that every entry of a totally unimodular matrix belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is totally unimodular precisely when every square subdeterminant is zero, one, or minus one.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite real matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff \det(A[I,J])\in\{-1,0,1\}\) for every \(I,J\) with \(|I|=|J|\).

notation.meaning: submatrix with row set I and column set J
determinant of a square matrix B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The determinantal definition and entrywise consequence are standard and correctly stated, but no inspectable source or explicit standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Ghouila-Houri Signed-Partition Criterion
children.top_down_role: The classical signed-partition recognition family.

children.title: Ghouila-Houri Criterion
children.top_down_role: The classical total-unimodularity recognition viewpoint associated with Ghouila-Houri.

knowledge_statements.title: Ghouila-Houri Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row-signing characterization of total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,-1,1\}^{m\times n}\). Then \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every subset \(R\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) of rows, there exists a signing \(\sigma:R\to\{-1,1\}\) such that every column \(j\) satisfies \[\sum_{i\in R}\sigma(i)A_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}.\] Equivalently, each \(R\) admits a partition \(R=R_+\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_-\) for which the sum of the rows in \(R_+\), minus the sum of the rows in \(R_-\), is componentwise in \(\{-1,0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-plus-minus-one matrix is totally unimodular exactly when every row subset can be signed so each signed column sum is zero or plus-minus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff \forall R\,\exists\sigma\,\forall j:\sum_{i\in R}\sigma(i)A_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}.\)

notation.meaning: an arbitrary subset of row indices
a plus-minus-one signing of the selected rows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The row-signing characterization is stated correctly and has the appropriate theorem kind, but the theorem has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Signed-Partition Certificates
children.top_down_role: Partition-based sign certificates used in total-unimodularity recognition.

knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Partition Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificates realizing the Ghouila-Houri predicate for specified row subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matrix \(A\in\{0,-1,1\}^{m\times n}\) and a specified row subset \(R\), a signed-partition certificate is a disjoint partition \(R=R_+\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_-\) satisfying \[\sum_{i\in R_+}A_{ij}-\sum_{i\in R_-}A_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}\qquad\text{for every column }j.\] The certificate is checked by computing these column sums. A family containing such a certificate for every row subset \(R\) certifies total unimodularity through the Ghouila-Houri criterion; a single partition certifies only the criterion for its specified subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition of a selected row set certifies its signed-sum condition; certificates for every row subset establish total unimodularity.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_+,R_-\) certify \(\left|\sum_{i\in R_+}A_{ij}-\sum_{i\in R_-}A_{ij}\right|\le 1\) for every \(j\).

notation.meaning: positive and negative parts of the selected row set
entry in row i and column j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between a certificate for one row subset and a family covering every subset is correct, and certificate is the proper content kind. An authoritative locator for the underlying criterion is missing.

children.title: Row-Signing Viewpoint
children.top_down_role: Matrix signing interpretations underlying the recognition criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Row-Signing Viewpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent vector formulation of the Ghouila-Houri signed partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(A\in\{0,-1,1\}^{m\times n}\) and a row subset \(R\). A partition \(R=R_+\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_-\) is equivalently represented by a vector \(y\in\{-1,0,1\}^m\) with \(y_i=1\) on \(R_+\), \(y_i=-1\) on \(R_-\), and \(y_i=0\) outside \(R\). Its signed column-sum vector is \(A^{\mathsf T}y\). Hence the Ghouila-Houri requirement for \(R\) is exactly the existence of such a vector with support \(R\) and \[A^{\mathsf T}y\in\{-1,0,1\}^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed row partition is a sign vector whose transpose product with the matrix has every coordinate in zero or plus-minus one.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a subset of the row indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\text{ satisfies the signed criterion}\iff\exists y:\operatorname{supp}(y)=R,\ y_i\in\{-1,1\}\text{ on }R,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\in\{-1,0,1\}^n.\)

notation.meaning: row-sign vector extended by zero outside R

children.title: Signed-Criterion Recognition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Practical limits of applying signed-partition criteria directly.

knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Criterion Recognition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes a complete characterization from direct efficient recognition by exhaustive checking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Ghouila-Houri condition is logically complete for total unimodularity, but its quantifier form alone is not a polynomial-time recognition algorithm. Direct verification considers up to \(2^m\) row subsets \(R\); naively searching a signing for each subset considers as many as \(2^{|R|}\) sign vectors. Thus exhaustive use has exponential worst-case work even though each proposed signed partition can be checked in polynomial time. Efficient total-unimodularity recognition requires additional structural or algorithmic machinery rather than enumeration of all signed-partition obligations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed criterion characterizes total unimodularity, but exhaustive enumeration of its row subsets and signings is exponential.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\{0,-1,1\}^{m\times n}\) is presented explicitly.
Recognition uses direct exhaustive evaluation of the criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Direct enumeration requires at least consideration of }2^m\text{ row-subset obligations in the worst case}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly limits its exponential-work claim to direct exhaustive evaluation and fits a failure-boundary container, but no source supports the recognition-complexity discussion.

children.title: Closure Operations for Total Unimodularity
children.top_down_role: Matrix transformations and compositions preserving total unimodularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Operations for Total Unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary matrix operations that preserve total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\) is totally unimodular, then each matrix obtained by transposing \(A\), permuting rows or columns, multiplying any row or column by \(-1\), deleting rows or columns, or duplicating a row or column is totally unimodular. Total unimodularity is also preserved when a zero row or column, or a row or column having exactly one nonzero entry equal to \(1\) or \(-1\), is appended. Consequently, adjoining identity columns or identity rows preserves total unimodularity. Each assertion concerns finite matrices and may be applied repeatedly in any order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transpose, permutations, sign changes, submatrices, duplications, and adjoining zero or signed unit rows or columns preserve total unimodularity.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite totally unimodular matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ totally unimodular}\implies T(A)\text{ totally unimodular}\) for every listed operation \(T\).

notation.meaning: matrix obtained from A by a listed closure operation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The listed elementary operations do preserve total unimodularity and the property kind fits the container, but the closure claims lack a cited source or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Decomposition-Based TU Recognition Interface
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic recognition and structural decomposition beyond elementary sufficient criteria.

children.title: Structural TU Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Decomposition viewpoints for assembling or analyzing totally unimodular matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural TU Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-matroid form of Seymour’s decomposition theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every regular matroid can be obtained by repeated \(1\)-, \(2\)-, and \(3\)-sums starting from graphic matroids, cographic matroids, and copies of the exceptional ten-element regular matroid \(R_{10}\). Conversely, every matroid assembled from these basic pieces by those sums is regular. Through totally unimodular representations, this yields a structural decomposition of total-unimodularity instances into network-type blocks, transposed network-type blocks, and the fixed exceptional block, subject to representation equivalences and compatible sum operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular matroids, and correspondingly TU representations, decompose through one-, two-, and three-sums into graphic, cographic, and one exceptional basic type.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid.
Regularity means representability over every field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is regular}\iff M\text{ is composed from graphic, cographic, and }R_{10}\text{ pieces by }1\text{-, }2\text{-, and }3\text{-sums}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regular-matroid decomposition claim is appropriately classified as a theorem, but this specialized result and its translation to TU representations require an authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Regular-Matroid Recognition Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between total-unimodularity recognition and regular-matroid structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular-Matroid Recognition Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connection between total-unimodular matrices and regular matroid representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M\) is regular if and only if it admits a totally unimodular real matrix representation. More concretely, if a binary representation is placed in standard form \([I\mid B]\), then \(M\) is regular if and only if the nonzero entries of \(B\) can be assigned signs so that the resulting signed matrix \(\widetilde B\) is totally unimodular; then \([I\mid\widetilde B]\) is a totally unimodular real representation of \(M\). Thus regular-matroid recognition supplies a structural interface for TU recognition, while the compatibility of a given matrix’s signs remains part of the matrix-level question.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular matroids are exactly those with TU representations; a binary standard representation must admit a compatible signing into a TU matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite binary matroid represented in standard form \([I\mid B]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is regular}\iff\exists\widetilde B\text{ obtained by signing the support of }B\text{ such that }[I\mid\widetilde B]\text{ is totally unimodular}.\)

notation.meaning: signed real matrix with the same support as B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed interface is plausible and appropriately classified as a representation, but the exact standard-form signing equivalence is specialized and unsupported by a source locator.

children.title: Decomposition-Based TU Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition organized through structural pieces and composition operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based TU Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive recognition template based on regular-matroid decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a matrix \(A\in\{0,-1,1\}^{m\times n}\). First reject if an elementary necessary condition fails. Convert an appropriate standard-form representation of \(A\) to its associated binary matroid and recursively search for valid \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum separations. At each leaf, test whether the component is graphic, cographic, or isomorphic to \(R_{10}\); also verify that the original signs are compatible with the reconstructed totally unimodular representation. Accept exactly when all leaves are basic regular pieces and every composition and signing check succeeds; otherwise reject. The output is a decision together with a decomposition tree when accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognition recursively decomposes the associated matroid, validates graphic, cographic, or exceptional leaves, and checks that the original matrix signs are compatible.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\{0,-1,1\}^{m\times n}\) is finite.
Subroutines correctly find sums and recognize the three basic piece types.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The procedure accepts }A\iff A\text{ is totally unimodular}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct knowledge kind, but correctness depends on unspecified standard-form conversion, separation, composition, and sign-compatibility procedures. A precise recognition-algorithm source is required.

children.title: Elementary-Criterion Boundary
children.top_down_role: Totally unimodular families not readily identified by elementary sufficient criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Elementary-Criterion Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entrywise and two-by-two determinant tests do not characterize total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Every entry of \(A\) belongs to \(\{0,1\}\), and every \(2\times2\) subdeterminant belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\). Nevertheless, \(\det(A)=-2\), so \(A\) is not totally unimodular. Therefore checking only the allowed entry set and all minors through order two is insufficient; higher-order structure, a complete signed criterion, or a decomposition-based test is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-by-three zero-one matrix can pass every entry and two-by-two minor test yet fail total unimodularity because its determinant is minus two.
assumptions_latex: Total unimodularity is tested by square subdeterminants of every order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det(A)=-2\), hence \(A\) is not totally unimodular despite all minors of order at most two lying in \(\{-1,0,1\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed matrix is a valid counterexample: its determinant is minus two while all minors of order at most two have allowed values. The counterexample kind fits the boundary container, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Canonical Totally Unimodular Matrix Families
children.top_down_role: Recurring matrix classes supplying exact LP relaxations.

children.title: Incidence-Network Matrix Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Graph-incidence and tree-based network matrix families.

children.title: Directed Node–Arc Incidence Matrices
children.top_down_role: Oriented graph-incidence matrices arising from directed networks.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonloop column contains one \(+1\), one \(-1\), and zeros elsewhere; every loop column is zero; moreover, \(D\) is totally unimodular.

notation.meaning: finite directed graph with node set V and arc set E

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard directed-incidence definition and total-unimodularity property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the head-positive, tail-negative incidence convention, permits parallel arcs and loops, and states the total-unimodularity property of the resulting matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), define its directed node–arc incidence matrix \(D\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times E}\) as follows. For every node \(v\) and nonloop arc \(e=(u,w)\), \[D_{ve}=\begin{cases}-1,&v=u,\\+1,&v=w,\\0,&v\notin\{u,w\}.\end{cases}\] A loop has a zero column. Thus every nonloop column has exactly one negative and one positive entry, whereas every loop column is zero. Every square subdeterminant of \(D\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\), so \(D\) is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed incidence column records minus one at a nonloop arc's tail and plus one at its head, while a loop gives a zero column. Every directed node–arc incidence matrix is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Node–Arc Incidence Matrices

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed node–arc incidence matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed incidence representation of a directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), the node--arc incidence matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times |E|}\) has one row per node and one column per arc. For each arc \((i,j)\in E\), its column is \(A_{\cdot,(i,j)}=e_i-e_j\), having \(+1\) in row \(i\), \(-1\) in row \(j\), and zeros elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed node–arc incidence matrix has one row per node and one column per arc. The column for an arc from i to j has +1 at i, −1 at j, and zero elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a digraph with }V=\{1,\ldots,m\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_{\cdot,(i,j)}=e_i-e_j\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in E.

source_evidence.locator: Minimal Cost Network Flows / 9.3. Properties of the A Matrix / Definition 9.3-extra-1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank of a connected digraph incidence matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank and spanning-tree column characterization for directed node–arc incidence matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be the node--arc incidence matrix of a digraph whose underlying undirected graph is connected and has \(m\ge 2\) nodes. Then \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m-1\). Moreover, if \(T\) is any set of \(m-1\) arcs whose underlying edges form a spanning tree, the columns \(A_T\) are linearly independent; after suitable row and column permutations and deletion of one row, they form a lower-triangular \((m-1)\times(m-1)\) matrix with diagonal entries in \(\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence matrix of a connected digraph with m nodes has rank m−1. The columns associated with any underlying spanning tree are independent and yield a nonsingular reduced square matrix.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is the node--arc incidence matrix of a digraph }G.
\text{The underlying undirected graph of }G\text{ is connected}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unimodularity and integrality of network incidence bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Triangular basis structure, integral basic solutions, and total unimodularity for directed node–arc incidence systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected minimum-cost network-flow incidence system augmented by one root arc, every rooted-spanning-tree basis \(B\) can be permuted into lower-triangular form with entries in \(\{-1,0,1\}\) and diagonal entries in \(\{-1,1\}\). Consequently \(\det B=\pm1\), and for \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), the solution of \(Bx_B=b\) is integral; hence the corresponding standard-form extreme points are integral. Moreover, the directed node--arc incidence matrix \(A\) is totally unimodular: every square submatrix \(A_{I,J}\) satisfies \(\det(A_{I,J})\in\{-1,0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rooted-tree network bases are triangular up to permutation with ±1 diagonal, so integer balance vectors produce integer basic solutions. Directed node–arc incidence matrices are totally unimodular: every square subdeterminant is −1, 0, or 1.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is the directed node--arc incidence matrix of a connected network}.
B\text{ is a rooted-spanning-tree basis of the system augmented by one root arc}.
b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\text{ for the basic-solution integrality conclusion}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \det B\in\{-1,1\},\qquad b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\Rightarrow B^{-1}b\in\mathbb{Z}^m,\qquad \det(A_{I,J})\in\{-1,0,1\}\text{ for every square }A_{I,J}.
