children.title: Tree-Based Network Matrices
children.top_down_role: Network matrices constructed relative to a spanning-tree basis.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is connected.
\(T\subseteq E\) is a spanning tree.
One row is deleted from the directed incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matrix \(M=B^{-1}N\) is a network matrix and is totally unimodular.

notation.meaning: nonsingular reduced-incidence submatrix indexed by tree arcs
reduced-incidence submatrix indexed by nontree arcs

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard spanning-tree definition of a network matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines network matrices through a spanning-tree basis of a reduced incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected directed graph, let \(T\subseteq E\) be a spanning tree, and delete one node row from the directed incidence matrix. Partition the resulting matrix as \([B\;N]\), where the columns of \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{(|V|-1)\times(|V|-1)}\) correspond to \(T\). Since \(B\) is nonsingular, the tree-based network matrix is \[M=B^{-1}N.\] Each column of \(M\) is the signed incidence vector of the unique tree path joining the endpoints of its nontree arc, and \(M\) is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing a spanning tree as a reduced-incidence basis gives the network matrix B inverse N; its columns encode signed fundamental tree paths, and it is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Based Network Matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spanning-tree construction, fundamental-path interpretation, and total-unimodularity assertion are mathematically standard and fit this leaf, but no source or specific locator is supplied. An authoritative network-matrix definition or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Incidence–Network Matrix Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between incidence representations and network-matrix representations.

assumptions_latex: \(D=[B\;N]\) is a reduced directed incidence matrix.
\(B\) consists of the columns of a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The row-equivalent form is \(B^{-1}D=[I\;M]\), where \(M=B^{-1}N\), and conversely every tree-based network matrix arises this way.

notation.meaning: reduced directed incidence matrix partitioned into tree and nontree columns

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard reduced-incidence basis representation of network matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the algebraic correspondence for a fixed spanning-tree basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[B\;N]\) be a reduced node–arc incidence matrix of a connected directed graph, with \(B\) the nonsingular submatrix indexed by a spanning tree. Multiplication by \(B^{-1}\) gives \[B^{-1}D=[I\;B^{-1}N]=[I\;M].\] Hence the nonidentity block in the tree-basis representation of a reduced incidence matrix is precisely its network matrix. Conversely, every tree-based network matrix \(M\) is obtained as \(B^{-1}N\) from such a reduced incidence matrix and spanning-tree partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pivoting a reduced incidence matrix on spanning-tree columns produces an identity block and a network-matrix block; every tree-based network matrix has this construction.
knowledge_statements.title: Incidence–Network Matrix Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation \(B^{-1}D=[I\;B^{-1}N]\) and its converse match the incidence–network correspondence leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation. A specific definition, proposition, or page locator supporting both directions is required.

children.title: Orientation Invariance
children.top_down_role: Effects of arc orientation choices on the relevant matrix class.

assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a directed node–arc incidence matrix.
\(S\) is diagonal with entries in \(\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reorienting arcs replaces \(D\) by \(DS\), which is totally unimodular exactly when \(D\) is.

notation.meaning: directed node-arc incidence matrix under an initial orientation
diagonal sign matrix identifying reversed arcs

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: column sign changes preserve all absolute subdeterminants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns arbitrary reversal of arcs in a fixed underlying graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an orientation of an undirected multigraph and let \(D\) be its directed node–arc incidence matrix. Reversing any selected set of arcs multiplies the corresponding columns by \(-1\); thus the new incidence matrix is \(D'=DS\), where \(S\) is diagonal and \(S_{ee}\in\{-1,1\}\). Every square subdeterminant of \(D'\) equals the corresponding subdeterminant of \(D\) times a sign. Consequently \(D'\) is totally unimodular if and only if \(D\) is, independently of the chosen orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing arcs only negates incidence columns. Column sign changes preserve absolute subdeterminants, so total unimodularity does not depend on orientation.
knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Invariance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orientation-invariance property is precise and mathematically standard, but the record supplies no citation or locator. A source addressing column sign changes or orientation invariance of incidence matrices is required.

children.title: Bipartite Incidence Matrices
children.top_down_role: Matrix structures underlying transportation and bipartite matching integrality.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)\) is a finite bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unsigned node–edge incidence matrix \(A\) is totally unimodular.

notation.meaning: bipartite graph with color classes U and W

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bipartite incidence becomes directed incidence after signing one color class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unsigned vertex–edge incidence matrix of a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph and define \(A\in\{0,1\}^{(U\cup W)\times E}\) by \(A_{ve}=1\) exactly when vertex \(v\) is incident to edge \(e\). Then every square subdeterminant of \(A\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\); equivalently, \(A\) is totally unimodular. In particular, linear systems using this incidence matrix and integral right-hand sides inherit the standard total-unimodularity integrality conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unsigned vertex–edge incidence matrix of every bipartite graph is totally unimodular, providing the matrix structure behind bipartite matching and transportation integrality.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Incidence Matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The total-unimodularity theorem for the unsigned incidence matrix of a bipartite graph fits the leaf and is standard. No source is cited, however, and the final statement about arbitrary linear systems is too broad unless the precise system form and integrality hypotheses are stated. A theorem locator and a qualified corollary are required.

children.title: Ordered-Interval Matrix Family

children.title: Consecutive-Ones Matrices
children.top_down_role: Binary matrix families admitting a consecutive nonzero ordering.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The consecutive-ones property holds exactly when some column permutation makes each row support an interval.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the row-wise property under a common permutation of columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) has the consecutive-ones property for rows if there exists a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that, for every row \(i\), the set \[\{k:A_{i,\pi(k)}=1\}\] is empty or equals \(\{\ell_i,\ell_i+1,\ldots,r_i\}\) for some \(1\leq \ell_i\leq r_i\leq n\). The same single column ordering must work simultaneously for all rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix has the row consecutive-ones property when one common column ordering makes the ones in every row form a single contiguous block.
knowledge_statements.title: Consecutive-Ones Matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The row-wise consecutive-ones definition is explicit, internally consistent, and appropriate for the leaf, but it lacks an authoritative citation with a definition or page locator.

children.title: Interval Matrices
children.top_down_role: Ordered matrix structures induced by intervals.

assumptions_latex: \((X,<)\) is a finite linearly ordered set.
\(\mathcal I\) is a family of intervals of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The incidence matrix \(A\) is an interval matrix and has consecutive ones in every row.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: incidence representation of intervals on a finite linear order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines rows as intervals and columns as ordered ground-set elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,<)\) be a finite linearly ordered set and let \(\mathcal I\) be a family of subsets of \(X\). The incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I\times X}\), defined by \(A_{Ix}=1\) if and only if \(x\in I\), is an interval matrix when every \(I\in\mathcal I\) is an order interval: whenever \(x<y<z\) and \(x,z\in I\), one also has \(y\in I\). Under the order of \(X\), every row of \(A\) therefore has consecutive ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval matrix records membership of points in intervals of one finite linear order; ordering columns by those points makes every row's ones consecutive.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interval-incidence construction is mathematically coherent and agrees with the stated row convention. Because interval-matrix terminology varies across sources, an authoritative definition with a specific locator is needed before accepting this candidate.

children.title: Column-Ordering Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of orderings that reveal consecutive-ones structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a valid consecutive-ones column ordering exactly when one exists.

notation.meaning: PQ-tree representing currently feasible column orders

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard PQ-tree reduction algorithm for consecutive-ones recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the classical PQ-tree recognition scheme for the row consecutive-ones property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), initialize a universal PQ-tree \(T\) whose frontiers are all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For rows \(i=1,\ldots,m\), set \(R_i=\{j:A_{ij}=1\}\) and reduce \(T\) by requiring the leaves in \(R_i\) to occur consecutively in every retained frontier. If a reduction fails, output that no consecutive-ones ordering exists. Otherwise, after all reductions, output any frontier \(\pi\) of \(T\); then every row support is consecutive under \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PQ-tree starts with all column orders and is reduced by each row support. Failure rejects the matrix; any final frontier is a valid consecutive-ones ordering.
knowledge_statements.title: Column-Ordering Recognition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind for this recognition leaf, and the high-level PQ-tree scheme states the intended success and failure behavior. Its correctness depends on the formal PQ-tree reduction operation, so a specific algorithmic source and theorem or section locator are required.

children.title: Interval–Ordering Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationships between interval representations and consecutive orderings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rows of \(A\) are intervals in some column order if and only if \(A\) has the consecutive-ones property for rows.

notation.meaning: a linear ordering of the columns

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct equivalence between interval set systems and consecutive-ones incidence matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies interval hypergraphs with row-consecutive binary incidence matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), let \(S_i=\{j:A_{ij}=1\}\). There exists a linear order \(\prec\) of the columns in which every \(S_i\) is an interval if and only if \(A\) has the consecutive-ones property for rows. Under such an order, \(A\) is the incidence matrix of the interval family \(\{S_1,\ldots,S_m\}\); conversely, ordering the columns by the ground-set order of any interval representation makes every row's ones consecutive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix admits a consecutive-ones column ordering exactly when its row supports can be represented as intervals of one common linear order.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval–Ordering Correspondence

children.title: Inequality-System Integrality Regime
children.top_down_role: The theorem family for inequality descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular.
\(b\in\mathbb Z^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is integral; in particular, every vertex of \(P\) is integral.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard total-unimodularity integrality theorem for inequality systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the pure inequality form with an integral right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular and let \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\). Then the rational polyhedron \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b\}\] is integral: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)+\operatorname{rec}(P)\). In particular, every vertex of \(P\), whenever vertices exist, belongs to \(\mathbb Z^n\). Thus every finite linear-programming optimum over \(P\) attained at a vertex has an integral optimal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A totally unimodular inequality matrix with an integral right-hand side defines an integral polyhedron, so all its vertices are integer vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Inequality-System Integrality Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inequality-system integrality theorem is standard and appropriately scoped to a totally unimodular matrix and integral right-hand side. No supporting source or specific theorem/page locator is supplied, so the theorem remains source-dependent candidate knowledge.

children.title: Equality-System Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integral-polyhedral consequences for equality-form systems.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular.
\(b\in\mathbb Z^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polyhedron \(Q=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) is integral.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard total-unimodularity integrality theorem for a nonnegative equality system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers standard-form equality systems with nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular and let \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\). Then \[Q=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\] is an integral polyhedron. Equivalently, every vertex of \(Q\), whenever vertices exist, belongs to \(\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a totally unimodular matrix and integral right-hand side, the nonnegative equality system defines an integral polyhedron and all of its vertices are integer vectors.

children.title: Lower-Bound Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Integrality behavior after adding or shifting variable lower bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular.
\(b\in\mathbb Z^m\) and \(\ell\in\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The substitution \(y=x-\ell\) converts \(Ax=b,\ x\geq\ell\) to \(Ay=b-A\ell,\ y\geq0\), and the original feasible polyhedron is integral.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integral translation reduces lower bounds to nonnegativity while preserving total unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Handles finite componentwise integral lower bounds by translation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular, \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and \(\ell\in\mathbb Z^n\). Define \[P_\ell=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq\ell\}.\] Under the integral translation \(y=x-\ell\), \[x\in P_\ell\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Ay=b-A\ell,\qquad y\geq0.\] The vector \(b-A\ell\) is integral, the coefficient matrix remains \(A\), and \(P_\ell\) is an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral lower bounds are represented by translating x by the lower-bound vector. The resulting nonnegative equality system has the same totally unimodular matrix, an integral shifted right-hand side, and an integral feasible polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Augmentation

children.title: Upper-Bound Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Integrality behavior after imposing variable upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of a totally unimodular equality system after adding integral upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,\pm1\}^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular and let \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\) and \(u\in\mathbb Z^n\). Then the augmented matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\ I&I\end{pmatrix}\) is totally unimodular. Consequently, every vertex of \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\] is integral. Equivalently, introducing the upper-bound slack \(s=u-x\) produces the equality system \(Ax=b\), \(x+s=u\), and \(x,s\ge0\), whose integral right-hand side and totally unimodular coefficient matrix imply \((x,s)\in\mathbb Z^{2n}\) at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral upper bounds may be added to a totally unimodular equality system without losing vertex integrality.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is totally unimodular.
\(b\) and \(u\) are integral.
\(P\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\).

notation.meaning: The equality-constrained polyhedron with lower and upper bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically precise and fits the upper-bound leaf, but no inspectable authoritative source or locator supports the TU augmentation and integrality consequence.

children.title: Bound-Transformation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interactions between equality descriptions, variable transformations, and bounded forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Transformation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine transformations reducing general integral bounds to nonnegative bounded variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(l,u\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(l\le u\), the substitution \(x=l+z\) gives the bijection \[\{x:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\longleftrightarrow\{z:Az=b-Al,\ 0\le z\le u-l\}.\] Complementing any coordinate \(j\) by \(x_j=u_j-z_j\) replaces column \(A_{\bullet j}\) by \(-A_{\bullet j}\) and adjusts the right-hand side by \(-u_jA_{\bullet j}\). If \(A\) is totally unimodular, these translations, column sign changes, and identity-column augmentations preserve the applicable totally unimodular regime; integral bounds also preserve integral right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral translations and variable complementation convert general bounds into standard bounds while preserving total unimodularity and integrality data.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular.
\(b,l,u\) are integral and \(l\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) and \(\{z:Az=b-Al,\ 0\le z\le u-l\}\) are affinely bijective, and corresponding vertices are simultaneously integral.

notation.meaning: Column j of the constraint matrix.

children.title: Primal Vertex Integrality

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Vertex Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-integrality consequence of total unimodularity for standard-form primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,\pm1\}^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular and \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\). For the standard-form polyhedron \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\] every vertex is integral. Hence, for any \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), if \(\min\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\) has a finite optimum attained at a vertex, it has an integral optimal solution. The conclusion concerns vertices and does not assert that every feasible point is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A totally unimodular standard-form system with an integral right-hand side has only integral vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is totally unimodular.
\(b\in\mathbb Z^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\).

notation.meaning: The set of vertices of P.

children.title: Integral Dual Optima
children.top_down_role: Dual optimization regimes admitting integral optimal solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Dual Optima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of an integral dual optimizer under total unimodularity and integral objective data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,\pm1\}^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular with full row rank, and let \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\). Define \[D=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:A^Ty\le c\}.\] Since \(A^T\) is totally unimodular and the right-hand side is integral, every vertex of \(D\) is integral. Therefore, for every \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), if \(\max\{b^Ty:y\in D\}\) is feasible and has a finite optimum, then it admits an optimal solution \(y^*\in\mathbb Z^m\). Full row rank excludes lineality and ensures a nonempty bounded optimal face contains a vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With full row rank, a totally unimodular dual constraint matrix and integral cost vector yield an integral dual optimum whenever the optimum is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is totally unimodular and has full row rank.
\(c\in\mathbb Z^n\).
The dual problem is feasible with finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in D} b^Ty\cap\mathbb Z^m\neq\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The full-row-rank hypothesis appropriately removes dual lineality and supports the integral-optimum conclusion, but the exact theorem lacks an inspectable source and locator.

children.title: Total Dual Integrality Boundary
children.top_down_role: The distinction between total unimodularity and stronger dual-integrality structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Total Dual Integrality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes matrix-based primal integrality from description-sensitive total dual integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Primal vertex integrality and total dual integrality are not properties of the same object: integrality is a property of a polyhedron, whereas total dual integrality is a property of a particular inequality description. Thus, from \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) being integral one cannot conclude that \(Ax\le b\) is totally dual integral. Moreover, multiplying a valid inequality by an integer \(k>1\) leaves its feasible halfspace unchanged but can destroy integral dual multipliers. For example, \(2x\le2\) describes the integral polyhedron \((-\infty,1]\), but for integral objective \(c=1\), its dual equality \(2y=1\), \(y\ge0\), has no integral feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral polyhedron need not have a TDI description; even scaling one inequality can destroy integral dual multipliers without changing the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: Total dual integrality is tested against every integral objective having a finite dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polyhedral integrality does not imply that an arbitrary defining system is totally dual integral.

notation.meaning: The dual multiplier associated with the displayed inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The description-sensitive TDI boundary and scaling counterexample are coherent and fit a failure-boundary container, but no authoritative TDI source is cited.

children.title: Primal–Dual Integrality Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationships between integral primal geometry and integral dual certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Integrality Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous integral primal and dual optima in a full-row-rank totally unimodular standard-form pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,\pm1\}^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular with full row rank, and let \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\). Consider \[\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\quad\text{and}\quad\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le c\}.\] If the primal problem is feasible and has a finite optimum, then there exist \(x^*\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n\) and \(y^*\in\mathbb Z^m\) that are respectively primal and dual optimal, satisfy \(c^Tx^*=b^Ty^*\), and obey complementary slackness \(x_j^*(c_j-A_{\bullet j}^Ty^*)=0\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral data and a full-row-rank totally unimodular matrix yield integral optimal solutions on both sides of the standard-form primal–dual pair.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is totally unimodular and has full row rank.
\(b\) and \(c\) are integral.
The primal is feasible with finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are integral optimal \(x^*,y^*\) with \(c^Tx^*=b^Ty^*\) and complementary slackness.

children.title: Total-Unimodularity Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of integral-polyhedron consequences through nonintegral data, side constraints, or weaker coefficient properties.

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Unimodularity Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failures caused by nonintegral data, non-TU side constraints, or weaker entry restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each principal hypothesis of the total-unimodularity integrality theorem matters. With the totally unimodular matrix \(A=(1)\) but nonintegral right-hand side \(b=1/2\), the equality system has the fractional vertex \(x=1/2\). Adding the side constraint \(2x\le1\) to \(0\le x\le1\) creates the fractional vertex \(x=1/2\). Finally, entries restricted to \(\{0,\pm1\}\) do not suffice: \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\] has determinant \(-2\), is not totally unimodular, and \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), has the fractional solution \(x=(1/2,1/2)^T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonintegral right-hand sides, incompatible side constraints, or merely small matrix entries can all invalidate the integral-vertex conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing integrality of the data or total unimodularity of the complete constraint system can produce fractional vertices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed counterexamples correctly illustrate the stated TU failure boundaries and the content kind fits, but the record supplies no evidence reference or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Alternative Integrality Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Integral-polyhedron mechanisms not exhausted by total unimodularity.

children.title: Total Dual Integrality
children.top_down_role: A description-sensitive dual route to integral polyhedra.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Total Dual Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for rational inequality descriptions in maximization form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational system \(Ax\le b\), with \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), is totally dual integral if, for every \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\) for which \[\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\}\] has a finite optimum, the dual problem \[\min\{b^Ty:A^Ty=c,\ y\ge0\}\] has an optimal solution \(y^*\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\). The definition belongs to the displayed system, not merely to its feasible polyhedron; different descriptions of the same polyhedron may differ in total dual integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A system is TDI when every finite LP with an integral objective has an integral optimal vector of dual multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b\) are rational.
\(c\) ranges over integral objective vectors with finite primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le b\) is TDI exactly when an integral optimal dual multiplier exists for every such \(c\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard description-sensitive definition of TDI in maximization form, but no authoritative definition locator is provided.

children.title: Integer Decomposition Properties
children.top_down_role: Integrality supported by decomposition of scaled or aggregate feasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Decomposition Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer decomposition property for rational polyhedra and their integral dilations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has the integer decomposition property if, for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every \(z\in kP\cap\mathbb Z^n\), there exist \(z^1,\ldots,z^k\in P\cap\mathbb Z^n\) such that \[z=z^1+\cdots+z^k.\] Here \(kP=\{kx:x\in P\}\). Thus every integral point representing a feasible aggregate of \(k\) identical copies decomposes into \(k\) integral points feasible for the unscaled polyhedron. The property is stronger than the mere existence of integral vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integral point in an integer dilation of an IDP polyhedron decomposes into the same number of integral points from the original polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(kP\cap\mathbb Z^n=(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)+\cdots+(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)\) for every \(k\ge1\), with \(k\) summands.

notation.meaning: The dilation of P by the positive integer k.
Integral points of the original polyhedron.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The IDP definition, quantifiers, dilation notation, and content kind are appropriate, but the definition lacks a cited authoritative locator.

children.title: Balanced-Perfect Matrix Interface
children.top_down_role: Matrix classes supporting exact packing, covering, and graph-model relaxations.

children.title: Balanced Matrices
children.top_down_role: Balanced matrix structure relevant to exact packing or covering relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard forbidden-submatrix definition for binary balanced matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is balanced if it contains no square submatrix of odd order in which every row and every column contains exactly two entries equal to \(1\). Equivalently, every square submatrix having exactly two ones in each row and column has even order. The condition is inherited by row and column deletion, because every forbidden submatrix of a deletion would already be a forbidden submatrix of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix is balanced when it has no odd square submatrix with exactly two ones in every row and column.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a binary matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is balanced precisely when all two-ones-per-row-and-column square submatrices have even order.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forbidden-submatrix definition of a balanced binary matrix is precise and locally appropriate, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Perfect Matrices
children.top_down_role: Perfect matrix structure associated with integral set-system polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfectness of a binary matrix defined through its set-packing polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), define the set-packing polyhedron \[Q(A)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n:Ax\le\mathbf1\}.\] The matrix \(A\) is perfect if \(Q(A)\) is an integral polyhedron, meaning every vertex of \(Q(A)\) lies in \(\mathbb Z^n\). Because \(x\ge0\) and each constrained coordinate is at most \(1\), integral feasible vertices are incidence vectors on all nonzero columns; zero columns may create unbounded directions without altering the vertex-integrality definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix is perfect when its fractional set-packing polyhedron has only integral vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a binary matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is perfect if and only if \(\operatorname{vert}(Q(A))\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\).

notation.meaning: The set-packing polyhedron associated with A.
The all-ones vector of the required dimension.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-packing definition is internally coherent, including its treatment of zero columns, but matrix-perfectness conventions vary and require a specific authoritative locator.

children.title: Set-Packing Integrality Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections from these matrix classes to exact set-packing relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Packing Integrality Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balancedness as a sufficient condition for integrality of the associated set-packing relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) be balanced. Then the set-packing polyhedron \[Q(A)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n:Ax\le\mathbf1\}\] is integral; equivalently, \(A\) is perfect. Consequently, for every objective \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) for which \(\max\{c^Tx:x\in Q(A)\}\) has a finite optimum, an integral optimal solution exists. When every column of \(A\) is nonzero, each integral point of \(Q(A)\) is a binary vector and represents a feasible set packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced binary matrices have integral set-packing relaxations, so every finite linear objective admits an integral optimal packing.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a balanced binary matrix.
The stated optimization problem has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vert}(Q(A))\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\), and an integral optimizer exists.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The balanced-matrix set-packing integrality theorem is correctly typed and scoped, but this nontrivial implication has no authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Graph-Relaxation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Graph-model relaxations distinguished by balancedness or perfection properties.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) if and only if \(G\) is perfect.

notation.meaning: Clique-inequality relaxation of the stable-set polytope.
Convex hull of incidence vectors of stable sets of G.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the clique relaxation characterization of perfect graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and define \(Q(G)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{V}:\sum_{v\in C}x_v\le 1\text{ for every clique }C\subseteq V\}\). Then \(Q(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\), and hence the clique relaxation is integral, if and only if \(G\) is perfect. Thus clique inequalities mark the graph-relaxation boundary: outside the perfect-graph class they need not describe the stable-set polytope; for example, an induced odd cycle of length at least five admits a fractional clique-feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative clique relaxation equals the stable-set polytope exactly for perfect graphs; induced odd holes exhibit failure beyond this boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Relaxation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically precise, matches the graph-relaxation boundary leaf, and uses the correct theorem content kind. However, no source is supplied for the perfect-graph polyhedral characterization, so the biconditional and its exact scope cannot be admitted under the evidence contract.

children.title: Polymatroid Integrality Interface
children.top_down_role: Integral LP structure arising from submodular rank systems.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(f:2^E\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) is normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{E}:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq E\}\) is integral.

notation.meaning: Sum of coordinates indexed by S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite integral polymatroids in inequality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) satisfy \(f(\varnothing)=0\), \(f(S)\le f(T)\) whenever \(S\subseteq T\), and \(f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T)\). The polymatroid \(P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{E}:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\}\) is an integral polyhedron. Equivalently, every nonempty face of \(P(f)\) contains an integral point, and every bounded linear optimization problem over \(P(f)\) has an integral optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized, nondecreasing, integer-valued submodular rank function defines an integral polymatroid polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Polymatroid Integrality Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite, normalized, nondecreasing, integer-valued submodular formulation is the standard polymatroid integrality theorem and fits the leaf and theorem container. No citation is supplied, however, so the integrality theorem and its stated equivalent consequences lack the required inspectable evidence.

children.title: Integrality Transformation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Operations that preserve integral structure and boundaries where it can be lost.

children.title: Elementary Integrality Preservation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Basic constructions inheriting integrality from component polyhedra.

children.title: Integral Faces
children.top_down_role: Face restrictions that inherit integral geometry from a parent polyhedron.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an integral polyhedron.
\(F\) is a nonempty face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{conv}(F\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\), so \(F\) is integral.

notation.meaning: An integral polyhedron in Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face inheritance for integral polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Extreme Points, Faces, Directions, and Extreme Directions of Polyhedral Sets: Geometric Insights p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be integral, meaning \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\), and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(P\). Then \(F=\operatorname{conv}(F\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\). In particular, every vertex of \(F\) is an integral vertex of \(P\), so passing from an integral polyhedron to any face preserves integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face of an integral polyhedron is itself integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Faces

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Extreme Points, Faces, Directions, and Extreme Directions of Polyhedral Sets: Geometric Insights p. 71

children.title: Variable-Fixing Preservation
children.top_down_role: Integrality behavior under restriction of selected variables.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq[0,1]^n\) is an integral polyhedron.
\(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(b\in\{0,1\}^{I}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\cap\{x:x_i=b_i\text{ for }i\in I\}\) is empty or integral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary variables fixed at their valid bounds; arbitrary integer slices are excluded.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Extreme Points, Faces, Directions, and Extreme Directions of Polyhedral Sets: Geometric Insights p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq[0,1]^n\) be integral, choose \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and prescribe \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(i\in I\). The set \(F=P\cap\{x:x_i=b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\) is either empty or a face obtained by successively imposing valid bound equalities. Consequently \(F\) is integral. This preservation claim does not extend to an arbitrary interior equality \(x_i=k\), which need not define a face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing binary coordinates of an integral 0-1 polyhedron to zero or one yields an empty set or an integral face.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Fixing Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Extreme Points, Faces, Directions, and Extreme Directions of Polyhedral Sets: Geometric Insights p. 71

children.title: Cartesian Product Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integral geometry of products formed from independent component polyhedra.

assumptions_latex: \(P_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) is integral for each \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1\times\cdots\times P_m\) is integral.

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of the component polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products in disjoint coordinate spaces.

source_refs.locator: 2.1. Polyhedra and convex sets p. 42

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(P_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) be integral. Then their Cartesian product \(P=P_1\times\cdots\times P_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_1+\cdots+n_m}\) is integral, with \(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n_1+\cdots+n_m}=(P_1\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n_1})\times\cdots\times(P_m\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n_m})\). If the factors are pointed, every vertex of \(P\) is a tuple of factor vertices and is therefore integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite Cartesian product of integral polyhedra in disjoint coordinates is integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian Product Integrality

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1. Polyhedra and convex sets p. 42

children.title: Product-Coupling Boundary
children.top_down_role: The transition from independent products to linked constructions that may lose integrality.

assumptions_latex: The product is intersected with the coupling equation \(x+2y=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P_1\times P_2)\cap\{(x,y):x+2y=1\}\) is not integral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single integral coupling equality can destroy product integrality.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Although \(P_1=P_2=[0,1]\) are integral, coupling their coordinates can destroy integrality. Indeed, \(R=(P_1\times P_2)\cap\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x+2y=1\}=\operatorname{conv}\{(1,0),(0,1/2)\}\). The point \((0,1/2)\) is a fractional vertex of \(R\). Hence Cartesian-product integrality alone gives no preservation guarantee after adding even one equality with integral coefficients and integral right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single linking equality can turn a product of integral intervals into a polytope with a fractional vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Coupling Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

children.title: Block-Coupling Integrality Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Interaction between independent blocks, linking structure, and integral geometry.

children.title: Independent Block Products
children.top_down_role: Integral geometry assembled from uncoupled block components.

assumptions_latex: Each block polyhedron \(P_i=\{x^i:A_i x^i\le b_i\}\) is integral.
Block coordinates are disjoint and no linking constraints or variables are present.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:A_i x^i\le b_i\text{ for all }i\}=\prod_i P_i\) is integral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncoupled block-diagonal systems in disjoint variables.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_i=\{x^i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}:A_i x^i\le b_i\}\) be integral for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), with pairwise disjoint variable blocks. The block-diagonal system \(P=\{(x^1,\ldots,x^m):A_i x^i\le b_i\text{ for every }i\}\) equals \(\prod_{i=1}^m P_i\) and is integral. Thus independent block composition preserves integrality without requiring a common total-unimodularity representation of all blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncoupled block-diagonal system is the Cartesian product of its blocks and remains integral when every block is integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Block Products

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

children.title: Linking-Row Effects
children.top_down_role: Integrality consequences of constraints coupling multiple blocks.

assumptions_latex: The uncoupled blocks are \([0,1]\) and \([0,1]\).
The integral linking inequality \(x+2y\le2\) is added.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([0,1]^2\cap\{(x,y):x+2y\le2\}\) is not integral.

notation.meaning: Polyhedron after adding the linking row.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary integral linking rows need not preserve block integrality.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with the independent integral blocks \(P_1=P_2=[0,1]\). Adding the single linking row \(x+2y\le2\) produces \(R=[0,1]^2\cap\{(x,y):x+2y\le2\}\). The point \((1,1/2)\) is a vertex of \(R\) and is fractional. Therefore integral coefficients and an integral right-hand side in a linking row do not by themselves preserve integrality; additional matrix structure is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One integral linking row can create a fractional vertex even when every uncoupled block is an integral interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Linking-Row Effects

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

children.title: Linking-Column Effects
children.top_down_role: Integrality consequences of variables shared across block systems.

assumptions_latex: Without the shared variable, the block matrix is the identity and the right-hand side is integral.
A nonnegative linking variable \(z\) has column \((2,2)^{\mathsf T}\).

notation.meaning: Variable whose column appears in multiple block rows.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An unrestricted column shared across blocks may destroy integrality.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(R=\{(x_1,x_2,z)\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^3:x_1+2z=1,\ x_2+2z=1\}\). Removing the shared column of \(z\) leaves two independent identity blocks with the integral solution \((x_1,x_2)=(1,1)\). With the linking column present, \(R=\operatorname{conv}\{(1,1,0),(0,0,1/2)\}\), so \((0,0,1/2)\) is a fractional vertex. Hence arbitrary linking columns do not preserve block integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared column can couple otherwise integral identity blocks and create a fractional endpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Linking-Column Effects

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

children.title: Block-Coupling Integrality Loss
children.top_down_role: Coupling patterns that create fractional structure despite integral components.

assumptions_latex: The uncoupled feasible region is a Cartesian product of integral polyhedra.
Coupling rows or columns are allowed without a total-unimodularity, TDI, or equivalent integrality condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integrality of the coupled formulation is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure fails under unrestricted cross-block linear coupling.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\prod_{i=1}^m P_i\) with every \(P_i\) integral. There is no general implication that \(P\cap\{x:Lx\le d\}\) is integral when \(L\) and \(d\) are integral but couple distinct blocks. For instance, \([0,1]^2\cap\{(x,y):x+2y\le2\}\) has the fractional vertex \((1,1/2)\). Integrality after coupling therefore requires an additional certificate such as total unimodularity, total dual integrality, or a problem-specific decomposition argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral blocks can lose integrality under unrestricted cross-block coupling; an additional structural certificate is necessary.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Coupling Integrality Loss

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 Block Diagonal or Angular Structure p. 361

children.title: Lifted-Projection Integrality Boundary
children.top_down_role: The distinction between integral lifted descriptions and their projected representations.

children.title: Integral Lifted Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Integral geometry in higher-dimensional representations.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is a polyhedron.
Its coordinate projection is \(P=\{x:\exists y\text{ with }(x,y)\in Q\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is an integral lifted polyhedron for \(P\) exactly when \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+p})\).

notation.meaning: Polyhedron in original and auxiliary coordinates.
Projection of Q onto original coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate lifts with integer lattices in both original and auxiliary variables.

source_refs.locator: 2.8. Projections of polyhedra: Fourier-Motzkin elimination* p. 70
2.7. Representation of bounded polyhedra* p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) be a polyhedron in original coordinates \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and auxiliary coordinates \(y\in\mathbb{R}^p\), and let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p\text{ such that }(x,y)\in Q\}\). The polyhedron \(Q\) is an integral lifted polyhedron for \(P\) when \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+p})\). This definition imposes integrality in the full lifted coordinate lattice, not merely on the projected \(x\)-coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral lifted polyhedron is an integral polyhedron in original-plus-auxiliary coordinates whose coordinate projection gives the target polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Lifted Polyhedra

source_witnesses.locator: 2.8. Projections of polyhedra: Fourier-Motzkin elimination* p. 70
2.7. Representation of bounded polyhedra* p. 67

children.title: Coordinate Projection Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integrality behavior under elimination of lifted coordinates.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is an integral polyhedron.
\(\pi_x(x,y)=x\) is the coordinate projection onto \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(\pi_x(Q)\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\), so \(\pi_x(Q)\) is integral.

notation.meaning: Projection onto the original coordinate block.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate projections, rather than arbitrary nonintegral linear maps.

source_refs.locator: 2.8. Projections of polyhedra: Fourier-Motzkin elimination* p. 70
2.7. Representation of bounded polyhedra* p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) be integral and let \(\pi_x:\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) retain the first \(n\) coordinates. Then \(P=\pi_x(Q)\) is a polyhedron and satisfies \(P=\operatorname{conv}(\pi_x(Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+p}))\). Since \(\pi_x(Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+p})\subseteq P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\), it follows that \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\). Thus coordinate projection preserves integrality, although it may obscure a compact inequality description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coordinate projection of an integral lifted polyhedron is integral, though its direct inequality description may be much larger.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Projection Integrality

source_witnesses.locator: 2.8. Projections of polyhedra: Fourier-Motzkin elimination* p. 70
2.7. Representation of bounded polyhedra* p. 67

children.title: Extended-Formulation Integrality
children.top_down_role: Relationships between integral extensions and represented polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Formulation Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality transfer through an integer coordinate projection of a lifted polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) be an integral polyhedron and let \(\pi_x(x,y)=x\) be the coordinate projection. If \(P=\pi_x(Q)\), then \[P=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\bigr),\] so \(P\) is integral. More generally, the conclusion holds for any integer linear map \(T\) when \(P=T(Q)\). Thus an integral extended formulation supplies an integrality certificate for its projected polyhedron, although integrality of \(P\) does not force every extension representing \(P\) to be integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral lifted polyhedron has an integral image under coordinate projection or any integer linear map; the converse fails for arbitrary extensions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\mathbb Z^{n+p})\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)\)

notation.meaning: coordinate projection onto the original variables

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate-projection claim and its integer-linear-map generalization are mathematically standard and fit the property container, but no evidence is cited. A source must also support the generalization, with the domain and codomain of T stated explicitly.

children.title: Projection-Description Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between an integral projected set and a nonintegral visible description.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Description Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates projected-set integrality from integrality properties of a chosen inequality description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Integrality is a property of the projected polyhedron, not of every matrix describing it. For example, \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R:2x\le 2,\ -x\le 0\}=[0,1]\] is integral, but its displayed constraint matrix \(A=(2,-1)^{\mathsf T}\) is not totally unimodular because it contains the entry \(2\). Consequently, projecting an integral extension can prove that \(P\) is integral without implying total unimodularity, or any analogous integrality-preserving property, for a selected description of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection can yield an integral polyhedron even when a chosen inequality matrix for that polyhedron is not totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is integral, while }A\text{ is not totally unimodular}\)

notation.meaning: matrix in the displayed inequality description

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example is self-checkable, correctly distinguishes polyhedral integrality from total unimodularity of a chosen description, and fits a failure-boundary container. It nevertheless lacks the external evidence required for this nontrivial boundary claim.

children.title: Block-Structured Decomposition Architecture
children.top_down_role: Large LP architectures in which limited coupling supports master–subproblem or generated-representation methods.

children.title: Block Matrix Geometries
children.top_down_role: Canonical matrix layouts exposing separability, shared variables, and linking restrictions.

children.title: Block-Diagonal Structure
children.top_down_role: Independent LP blocks without cross-block restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\in\mathbb N\). For each \(i=1,\ldots,k\), let \(x_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}\), \(c_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}\), \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n_i}\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i}\). A linear program has block-diagonal structure if, after row and column permutations, it can be written as \[\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^{\mathsf T}x_i:A_i x_i=b_i,\ x_i\ge 0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,k\right\}.\] Equivalently, its constraint matrix is \(\operatorname{diag}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\). No constraint contains variables from two distinct blocks, and its feasible region is \(X_1\times\cdots\times X_k\), where \(X_i=\{x_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}:A_i x_i=b_i,\ x_i\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-diagonal LP has an additive objective, no cross-block constraints, and a feasible region equal to the Cartesian product of its local feasible polyhedra.

children.title: Primal Block-Angular Structure
children.top_down_role: Independent local blocks coupled by linking rows.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Block-Angular Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent local feasible sets coupled by common linking rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear program has primal block-angular structure if it admits the form \[\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^{\mathsf T}x_i:\sum_{i=1}^k B_i x_i=b_0,\ A_i x_i=b_i,\ x_i\ge0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,k\right\}.\] The diagonal rows \(A_i x_i=b_i\) define independent local polyhedra, while the linking rows \(\sum_i B_i x_i=b_0\) are the only constraints involving more than one variable block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal block-angular LP consists of independent local systems joined only by a common set of linking constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\)
\(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_i x_i=b_i\text{ are local rows and }\sum_i B_i x_i=b_0\text{ are linking rows}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal block-angular structure and separable pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP structure consisting of linking rows and block-diagonal local rows, together with its Dantzig–Wolfe subproblem consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \max\{cx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\} with the rows partitioned as A'x=b' and A''x=b''. The formulation is primal block-angular when, after a compatible partition of the variables, A'' is block diagonal and A'x=b' supplies the linking constraints. Consequently, for any pricing vector c', the subproblem \max\{c'x:A''x=b'',\ x\ge0\} separates into independent LPs over the diagonal blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal block-angular LP has block-diagonal local constraints coupled only by linking constraints. Its Dantzig–Wolfe pricing problem therefore splits into independent local problems.
assumptions_latex: Ax=b\text{ is partitioned into }A'x=b'\text{ and }A''x=b''
A''\text{ is block diagonal under a compatible variable partition}
x\ge0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{c'x:A''x=b'',\ x\ge0\}\text{ decomposes into independent optimization problems over the diagonal blocks.}

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Block-Angular Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local row systems coupled through a shared block of variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear program has dual block-angular structure if its variables can be partitioned as a shared vector \(z\) and local vectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), and it can be written as \[\min\left\{d^{\mathsf T}z+\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^{\mathsf T}x_i:D_i z+A_i x_i=b_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,k,\ z\ge0,\ x_i\ge0\right\}.\] Each row block contains its own local variables \(x_i\), while the complicating variables \(z\) occur in multiple row blocks and provide the sole cross-block coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual block-angular LP has separate local row systems coupled only through variables shared across those systems.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\)
\(x_i\text{ occurs only in row block }i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\text{ is the shared coupling block}\)

children.title: Bordered Block Matrices
children.top_down_role: Block systems with a core diagonal structure plus coupling borders.

knowledge_statements.title: Bordered Block Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-diagonal matrices augmented by coupling rows, columns, or both.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix is bordered block diagonal if row and column permutations put it in the form \[M=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0&\cdots&0&C_1\\0&A_2&\cdots&0&C_2\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&A_k&C_k\\R_1&R_2&\cdots&R_k&D\end{pmatrix}.\] The matrices \(A_i\) are diagonal blocks; the final block row and block column form the border. Deleting that border leaves \(\operatorname{diag}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\), so all interblock nonzeros are confined to the border.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bordered block matrix becomes block diagonal after deleting designated coupling rows and columns.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\)
\(M\text{ is partitioned conformably}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ minus its border equals }\operatorname{diag}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed doubly bordered block-diagonal form is coherent and fits a definition container, but bordered-matrix terminology varies as to whether the border consists of rows, columns, or both. An authoritative source with a specific locator is needed to establish the intended convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block-angular linear programming form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bordered block-diagonal LP representation in which disjoint local constraint systems are coupled by master equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the variables be partitioned into disjoint blocks $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, with $X_i=\{x_i:B_i x_i\le b_i,\ x_i\ge 0\}$. The associated block-angular linear program is represented as
\[
\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_T}\ \sum_{i=1}^T c_i^{\mathsf T}x_i
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^T A_i x_i=b,\qquad x_i\in X_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,T).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-angular linear program partitions the variables into disjoint blocks with independent local linear constraints and nonnegativity restrictions. Master equality constraints couple the blocks, while the objective is the sum of their local linear objectives.
assumptions_latex: T\in\mathbb{N}
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)\text{ is partitioned into disjoint variable blocks}
X_i=\{x_i:B_i x_i\le b_i,\ x_i\ge 0\}\quad(i=1,\ldots,T)
A_i,B_i,c_i,b_i,b\text{ have conformable dimensions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^T c_i^{\mathsf T}x_i:\sum_{i=1}^T A_i x_i=b,\ x_i\in X_i\ (i=1,\ldots,T)\right\}

children.title: Staircase Block Matrices
children.top_down_role: Sequential block systems with localized coupling across adjacent stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Staircase Block Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered block matrices with nonzeros confined to adjacent stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A block matrix has lower bidiagonal staircase form if, after compatible row and column permutations, \[M=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0&\cdots&0\\B_2&A_2&\ddots&\vdots\\0&B_3&\ddots&0\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&A_k\end{pmatrix}.\] Thus block row \(i\) may involve variables from stages \(i-1\) and \(i\), but no other stages. The transpose gives the upper-staircase convention. Wider staircase bandwidth is obtained by allowing a fixed number of neighboring block diagonals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A staircase matrix orders blocks by stage and restricts nonzeros to each stage and a bounded number of neighboring stages.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\)
\(M\text{ has a conformable ordered block partition}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{ij}=0\text{ whenever }j\notin\{i-1,i\}\)

notation.meaning: block in block row i and block column j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bidiagonal example is internally consistent, but the title is broader than that orientation and staircase bandwidth conventions vary. A source is required to determine whether the intended leaf covers only the displayed bidiagonal form or a wider class.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Staircase Multistage Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the staircase multistage structure. The preceding block-angular formulation supplies context but is not part of this node-owned definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multistage or staircase system is a linear system in stage vectors \(X_1,\ldots,X_T\) whose successive row blocks couple adjacent stages, with interior equations of the form \(\bar A_{t-1}X_{t-1}+A_tX_t=e_t\). A terminal equation may additionally contain \(P_0x_0\), where \(x_0\) is maximized. Activities of a period are therefore connected directly only with those of the preceding and following periods. The matrices \(A_t\), and likewise the matrices \(\bar A_t\), may be constant across stages, but such constancy is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multistage, or staircase, system has successive constraint blocks that couple only adjacent stages. Its terminal constraint may also contain the maximized variable x0. Stage matrices may repeat, but equality of the matrices across stages is not assumed.
assumptions_latex: T\in\mathbb N
X_t\text{ are stage vectors, and }A_t,\bar A_t,e_t,P_0\text{ have compatible dimensions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The system has staircase structure with coupling localized to adjacent stages.}

children.title: Nested Block Matrices
children.top_down_role: Hierarchical block systems with recursively embedded coupling structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Block Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive block structure indexed by a rooted hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix has nested block structure with respect to a rooted tree \(T\) if its rows and columns are assigned to nodes of \(T\), and every nonzero block \(M_{uv}\) satisfies that \(u\) and \(v\) are comparable in the ancestor order. Equivalently, blocks belonging to two disjoint subtrees have zero interaction after conditioning on their common ancestors. Each principal submatrix induced by a subtree therefore has the same form recursively, with coupling to the remainder occurring only through ancestor blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested block matrix follows a rooted hierarchy: disjoint subtrees do not interact directly, and every subtree repeats the same structural rule.
assumptions_latex: \(T\text{ is a finite rooted tree}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{uv}\neq0\Longrightarrow u\preceq_T v\text{ or }v\preceq_T u\)

notation.meaning: block indexed by tree nodes u and v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ancestor-comparability rule defines a coherent tree-indexed sparsity pattern, but it is not a universal definition of a nested block matrix. The claimed conditioning equivalence is also informal. A source is needed to identify and support the intended nested-block model.

children.title: Hierarchical Sparsity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sparsity patterns shared across multilevel or temporally ordered block forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Sparsity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-separator condition for multilevel block sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the variables and constraints of an LP be assigned to nodes of a rooted tree \(T\). The constraint matrix \(A\) has hierarchical sparsity if every nonzero coefficient \(A_{rv}\) joins a constraint node \(r\) and variable node \(v\) that lie on a common root-to-leaf path. Hence, for every node \(t\), row-variable interactions between distinct child subtrees of \(t\) are absent; any coupling between those subtrees is represented only by data assigned to \(t\) or its ancestors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hierarchical sparsity permits interactions along ancestor paths but excludes direct interactions between distinct child subtrees.
assumptions_latex: \(T\text{ is a finite rooted tree}\)
\(A\text{ has tree-indexed rows and columns}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_{rv}\neq0\Longrightarrow r\text{ and }v\text{ lie on a common root-to-leaf path of }T\)

notation.meaning: coefficient joining constraint r and variable v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common-root-to-leaf-path condition is mathematically coherent and the condition content kind fits the leaf, but hierarchical sparsity has several inequivalent tree and separator formulations. A specific authoritative source is needed to support this selected regime.

children.title: Dantzig–Wolfe Representation Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Dantzig–Wolfe Representation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point, ray, and mixed representations of pointed block polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonempty pointed polyhedron \(X_i\), let \(V_i\) and \(R_i\) be its finite sets of extreme points and extreme rays. Every \(x_i\in X_i\) has a representation \[x_i=\sum_{v\in V_i}\lambda_{iv}v+\sum_{r\in R_i}\mu_{ir}r,\qquad \sum_{v\in V_i}\lambda_{iv}=1,\qquad \lambda_{iv},\mu_{ir}\ge0.\] If \(X_i\) is bounded, \(R_i=\varnothing\); if it is unbounded, ray columns are retained. Substitution into linking constraints and the objective produces the Dantzig–Wolfe master representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each pointed block polyhedron is represented by convex combinations of extreme points plus nonnegative combinations of extreme rays, yielding bounded, unbounded, or mixed masters.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\text{ is a nonempty pointed polyhedron}\)
\(V_i=\operatorname{ext}(X_i)\)
\(R_i\text{ generates }\operatorname{rec}(X_i)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_i=\operatorname{conv}(V_i)+\operatorname{cone}(R_i)\)

notation.meaning: extreme points of block polyhedron i
extreme rays of block polyhedron i

children.title: Full Master LP
children.top_down_role: The complete coordinating LP over all represented columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Full Master LP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dantzig–Wolfe master containing every extreme-point and extreme-ray column.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{\sum_i c_i^{\mathsf T}x_i:\sum_i B_i x_i=b_0,\ x_i\in X_i\}\), where each \(X_i\) is a nonempty pointed polyhedron with extreme points \(V_i\) and extreme rays \(R_i\). Its full master LP is \[\min\sum_i\left(\sum_{v\in V_i}c_i^{\mathsf T}v\,\lambda_{iv}+\sum_{r\in R_i}c_i^{\mathsf T}r\,\mu_{ir}\right)\] subject to \[\sum_i\left(\sum_{v\in V_i}B_i v\,\lambda_{iv}+\sum_{r\in R_i}B_i r\,\mu_{ir}\right)=b_0,\quad \sum_{v\in V_i}\lambda_{iv}=1,\quad \lambda_{iv},\mu_{ir}\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full master substitutes all extreme points and rays of every local polyhedron into the linking constraints and objective.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\text{ is a nonempty pointed polyhedron}\)
\(X_i=\operatorname{conv}(V_i)+\operatorname{cone}(R_i)\)
\(\sum_i B_i x_i=b_0\text{ are the linking equations}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The full master and the original block-angular LP have the same feasible images and optimal value}\)

notation.meaning: all extreme points and extreme rays of block i

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted Master LP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-column restriction of the full Dantzig–Wolfe master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose nonempty subsets \(\widehat V_i\subseteq V_i\) and subsets \(\widehat R_i\subseteq R_i\). The restricted master LP is obtained from the full master by retaining only variables \(\lambda_{iv}\) for \(v\in\widehat V_i\) and \(\mu_{ir}\) for \(r\in\widehat R_i\), while preserving the linking equations, convexity equations \(\sum_{v\in\widehat V_i}\lambda_{iv}=1\), nonnegativity, and corresponding objective coefficients. Its feasible set embeds into that of the full master; therefore, for minimization, its optimal value is an upper bound on the full-master value whenever the restriction is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restricted master keeps selected point and ray columns; when feasible, its minimization value cannot be below the full-master optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\neq\widehat V_i\subseteq V_i\)
\(\widehat R_i\subseteq R_i\)
\(\text{the restricted master is feasible}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{RMP}}\ge z_{\mathrm{full}}\)

children.title: Stabilized Master LP
children.top_down_role: Master organizations designed to control dual movement or oscillation.

assumptions_latex: For each block \(k\), the current column set \(R_k\) is finite and nonempty.
A dual center \(\bar\pi\in\mathbb R^m\) and finite bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfy \(\ell\le \bar\pi\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed box-constrained dual is a linear-programming stabilization of the restricted master problem.

notation.meaning: Coupling dual multiplier and block convexity multipliers.
Cost and coupling column for column r of block k.
Componentwise trust box around the dual center.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects the box-step LP version of dual stabilization, rather than quadratic or bundle stabilization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given restricted column sets \(R_k\), the box-step stabilized master LP is the dual linear program
\[
\max_{\pi,\sigma}\; b^{\mathsf T}\pi+\sum_k\sigma_k
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
 a_{kr}^{\mathsf T}\pi+\sigma_k\le c_{kr}\quad(k,\ r\in R_k),
\qquad \bar\pi-\ell\le\pi\le\bar\pi+u.
\]
The box limits movement of the coupling multiplier while retaining every restricted-master dual inequality. Removing the box, equivalently taking infinite componentwise radii, recovers the ordinary restricted-master dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box-step stabilized master restricts restricted-master dual multipliers to a trust box around a center while preserving all current column inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Stabilized Master LP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The specialized box-step formulation needs an authoritative stabilization source. Moreover, ell and u are described simultaneously as absolute bounds and as radii around the center; these interpretations yield different boxes and must be reconciled.

children.title: Master-Restriction Correspondence

assumptions_latex: Each full block column set \(P_k\) contains the restricted set \(R_k\).
Both full and restricted master minimization problems are feasible and have finite optimal values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restricted-master value satisfies \(z_R\ge z_F\), while its dual feasible region contains the full-master dual feasible region.

notation.meaning: Full and restricted column sets for block k.
Optimal values of the full and restricted master minimization LPs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the full master minimize \(\sum_{k,r\in P_k}c_{kr}\lambda_{kr}\) subject to the coupling equations, the block convexity equations \(\sum_{r\in P_k}\lambda_{kr}=1\), and \(\lambda\ge0\). Replacing each \(P_k\) by \(R_k\subseteq P_k\) restricts the primal feasible set, hence \(z_R\ge z_F\). Dually, the restricted master retains only inequalities indexed by \(R_k\), so every full-master dual feasible point is restricted-master dual feasible. Equality \(z_R=z_F\) holds whenever an optimal full-master solution uses only columns in the restricted sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting available columns can only raise a minimization master value; dually, it removes inequalities. Equality holds when restricted columns support a full-master optimum.

children.title: Pricing Subproblem Family
children.top_down_role: Independent, structured, exact, and inexact local optimization interfaces for column discovery.

assumptions_latex: The decomposed master has block column sets \(P_k\), coupling multipliers \(\pi\), and block convexity multipliers \(\sigma_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pricing interfaces search for columns minimizing block reduced cost and report improving columns or valid lower-bound information.

notation.meaning: Feasible columns or extreme points of block k.
Reduced cost of block column r at master dual multipliers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers independent exact, structured, and approximate block oracles used for column discovery.

source_refs.locator: 6.1. Delayed column generation p. 232

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For block \(k\), a pricing interface receives restricted-master dual multipliers \((\pi,\sigma_k)\) and addresses
\[
q_k(\pi,\sigma_k)=\min_{r\in P_k}\bigl(c_{kr}-\pi^{\mathsf T}a_{kr}-\sigma_k\bigr).
\]
An exact interface returns a minimizer and the value \(q_k\). An inexact interface returns a feasible column, and may additionally return a certified lower bound on \(q_k\). A returned column is improving for a minimization master when its reduced cost is negative; blockwise lower bounds are required to certify the absence of materially improving omitted columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each pricing oracle minimizes reduced cost within one block, exactly or approximately, and returns improving columns or certified information about omitted columns.
knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Subproblem Family
