children.title: Certificate Use in Search
children.top_down_role: Interfaces through which LP certificates inform pruning and bounding decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Use in Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe pruning rules for minimization branch-and-bound nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization search node \(t\) whose LP relaxation has feasible region \(P_t\), and let \(U\) be the objective value of a known integer-feasible incumbent. The node may be pruned if an exact certificate proves \(P_t=\varnothing\). If instead a dual-feasible LP solution certifies a lower bound \(L_t\) satisfying \(L_t\ge U\), the node may also be pruned, because every integer-feasible descendant belongs to \(P_t\) and has objective value at least \(L_t\). Without one of these certificates or a valid integral-node conclusion, pruning is not justified solely by solver status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search safely discards a node when a verifiable LP certificate proves infeasibility or proves that its best possible objective cannot beat the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
Every descendant's integer-feasible set is contained in \(P_t\).
\(U\) is the value of an integer-feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(P_t=\varnothing\) or \(L_t\ge U\) is a valid certificate-based pruning condition.

notation.meaning: LP relaxation feasible region at node t

review_flags: authoritative branch-and-bound pruning locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimization pruning rules are correctly scoped and the principle content kind fits, but no authoritative branch-and-bound source and specific locator are supplied.

children.title: Numerically Fragile Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificate regimes vulnerable to scaling, tolerances, or numerical error.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerically Fragile Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small certificate margins are not robust to data or arithmetic errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), the system \(x\le0\), \(-x\le-\varepsilon\) is infeasible and has Farkas certificate \(y=(1,1)\), with annihilation residual zero and contradiction margin \(-b^{\mathsf T}y=\varepsilon\). Changing the second right-hand side from \(-\varepsilon\) to \(0\) produces the feasible system \(x=0\). Thus certificates with margin comparable to input uncertainty can change validity under an admissible perturbation. More generally, an approximate multiplier with nonzero \(A^{\mathsf T}y\) is not an exact certificate unless residual and data-error bounds imply a rigorous contradiction over the variable domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasibility certificate with a tiny contradiction margin can become invalid after equally tiny data perturbations, while an uncontrolled multiplier residual prevents exact certification.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
Right-hand-side uncertainty may be as large as \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A margin of size \(\varepsilon\) is insufficient for perturbation-robust infeasibility certification at uncertainty radius \(\varepsilon\).
review_flags: numerical certification and residual-bound source required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly illustrates loss of robustness at a perturbation equal to the certificate margin, and the failure-boundary kind fits. The broader claim about approximate residuals requires a source specifying rigorous residual, data-error, and variable-domain bounds.

children.title: Related-LP Reoptimization
children.top_down_role: Basis, dual, interior, and first-order reuse across closely related relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Related-LP Reoptimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-start algorithm for a sequence of closely related standard-form LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a sequence \(\min\{c_k^{\mathsf T}x:A_kx=b_k,\ x\ge0\}\) and a basis or primal-dual iterate from problem \(k-1\). Initialize problem \(k\) with that state after mapping unchanged rows and columns. For a candidate basis \(B\), compute \(x_B=B^{-1}b_k\) and reduced costs \(r_N=c_{k,N}-A_{k,N}^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}c_{k,B}\). If \(x_B\ge0\) and \(r_N\ge0\), return the associated optimum. Otherwise perform primal or dual simplex pivots according to the violated side; if the inherited state cannot supply the required feasibility, invoke a feasibility-restoration phase. Stop with an optimal solution or a valid infeasibility or unboundedness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reuse a prior basis or primal-dual state, test its feasibility and optimality for the modified LP, then repair it by pivots or feasibility restoration.
assumptions_latex: Successive LPs have compatible mapped variables and constraints.
Each candidate basis matrix is tested for nonsingularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns an optimum or a valid terminal LP certificate for each related instance.

source_refs.locator: 6. Large scale optimization p. 231

children.title: Weak-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: LP relaxation regimes providing limited objective-bound improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute integrality-gap definition for a minimization relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(X\) is the mixed-integer feasible set and \(P\) is its LP relaxation. For objective \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\min_{x\in X}c^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), assuming both values are finite. At tolerance \(\delta\ge0\), the instance is in a weak-bound regime when \[z_{\mathrm{IP}}-z_{\mathrm{LP}}>\delta.\] For scale-dependent comparisons, \(\delta\) must be fixed by an explicit normalization; the unnormalized inequality defines only the absolute-gap version.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimization LP bound is weak at tolerance delta when its lower bound lies more than delta below the mixed-integer optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Both optimization values are finite.
\(\delta\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The absolute weak-bound predicate is \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}-z_{\mathrm{LP}}>\delta\).
review_flags: terminology and normalization convention require a supporting source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The absolute-gap predicate is internally precise and definition is the correct kind, but the use of “weak-bound regime” and its tolerance convention require a supporting source with a specific locator.

children.title: Fractional Vertex Proliferation
children.top_down_role: Relaxation geometry containing extensive fractional extreme-point structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Vertex Proliferation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product family with exponentially many fractional LP vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,\tfrac12)\}\) and define \(P_k=Q^k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2k}\), with every coordinate required to be integral in the underlying mixed-integer model. Vertices of a Cartesian product are products of factor vertices, so \(P_k\) has \(3^k\) vertices. Exactly \(2^k\) select only \((0,0)\) or \((1,0)\) in every factor and are integral. Consequently, \(3^k-2^k\) vertices are fractional. Hence a compact product relaxation can exhibit exponentially many fractional vertices even though its integer-feasible vertices also have a simple product structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product of small triangular relaxations has 3^k vertices, of which 3^k−2^k are fractional, demonstrating exponential fractional-vertex proliferation.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is a positive integer.
All \(2k\) coordinates are integer-constrained in the discrete model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_k\) has exactly \(3^k-2^k\) fractional vertices.
review_flags: constructed family is self-contained but requires external source or independent review

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product construction and vertex count are mathematically consistent, and counterexample fits the leaf. No external source, evidence record, or explicit standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Bound–Fractionality Coupling
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between poor bounds and persistent fractional solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound–Fractionality Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractionality and objective-bound weakness do not imply one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is no universal quantitative implication between fractional optimal solutions and integrality-gap size. First, relaxing \(x\in\{0,1\}\) to \(x\in[0,1]\) for the objective \(\min 0\) gives zero integrality gap while every \(x\in(0,1)\) is an LP optimum. Second, for any \(M>0\), the model \(\min Mx\) subject to \(x\in\{0,1\}\) and \(x\ge\tfrac12\) has integer value \(M\), whereas its LP relaxation has the unique optimum \(x=\tfrac12\) and value \(M/2\). Its absolute gap \(M/2\) is arbitrarily large although only one variable is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional optimal points can coexist with zero gap, while one fractional variable can produce an arbitrarily large absolute gap; neither measure controls the other.
assumptions_latex: The examples use minimization and the absolute integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither the presence nor the count of fractional optimal variables universally bounds \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}-z_{\mathrm{LP}}\).
review_flags: self-contained counterexamples require external source or independent review

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two examples correctly separate fractionality from absolute integrality-gap magnitude, and counterexample is the correct kind. A source or admissible evidence rationale is still required.

children.title: Search Proliferation Consequences
children.top_down_role: Search growth associated with weak relaxation information.

knowledge_statements.title: Search Proliferation Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional node-count lower bound for binary branch-and-bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a binary branch-and-bound search through depth \(d\). Suppose that every generated node of depth less than \(d\) has a feasible fractional LP optimum, its certified bound does not permit incumbent pruning, and branching creates two feasible children. Then no node above depth \(d\) can be removed by infeasibility, integrality, or bound pruning. The search must therefore generate the complete binary tree through depth \(d\), containing \[1+2+\cdots+2^d=2^{d+1}-1\] nodes. Thus persistently weak bounds coupled with persistent fractionality can force exponential search growth, although either phenomenon alone does not establish this conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If weak bounds and fractional solutions prevent every standard pruning rule through depth d, binary branch-and-bound generates 2^(d+1)−1 nodes.
assumptions_latex: Branching is binary through depth \(d\).
Every node above depth \(d\) has two feasible children.
No infeasibility, integrality, or bound pruning applies above depth \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least \(2^{d+1}-1\) nodes are generated through depth \(d\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the explicit no-pruning and binary-branching assumptions, the node count is correct and complexity_bound fits the terminal container. No branch-and-bound complexity source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Degeneracy-Dual Instability Coupling
children.top_down_role: Degenerate geometry impairing inference and reoptimization.

children.title: Relaxation Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate relaxation structure affecting basis choice and local inference.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal degeneracy of a standard-form LP basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\). A basic feasible solution associated with a nonsingular basis matrix \(B\) has \(x_B=B^{-1}b\ge0\) and \(x_N=0\). It is degenerate when at least one basic component is zero. Equivalently, the solution has fewer than \(m\) strictly positive components. A relaxation is degenerate at an optimum when at least one optimal basic feasible solution is degenerate; this does not by itself imply that the optimal primal point or objective value is nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic feasible LP solution is degenerate when a basic variable equals zero, equivalently when fewer than m components are strictly positive.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\).
\(B\) is a nonsingular basis matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy holds exactly when some component of \(B^{-1}b\) is zero.
review_flags: standard definition lacks a supplied degeneracy-specific locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard-form degeneracy definition and its equivalence are correct, and definition fits the leaf. A degeneracy-specific authoritative locator is absent.

children.title: Dual-Solution Instability
children.top_down_role: Volatile or nonunique dual information across closely related LP solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Solution Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily small right-hand-side changes can select distant dual optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(b=(b_1,b_2)\), consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}x\) subject to \(x\ge b_1\) and \(x\ge b_2\). Its dual is \(\max b_1y_1+b_2y_2\) subject to \(y_1+y_2=1\) and \(y\ge0\). At \(b=(0,0)\), every point of the dual simplex is optimal. For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the perturbation \(b=(\varepsilon,0)\) uniquely selects \(y=(1,0)\), while \(b=(0,\varepsilon)\) uniquely selects \(y=(0,1)\). Thus arbitrarily close LP data can have dual optimizers a fixed positive distance apart, despite continuous optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate parameter value, tiny right-hand-side perturbations can select dual solutions a fixed distance apart even though the optimal value changes continuously.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
The scalar primal variable is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal-dual-solution mapping is not single-valued or continuous at \(b=(0,0)\).

children.title: Reoptimization Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Effects of degeneracy on warm starts and repeated LP solution behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Reoptimization Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact critical-region test for retaining a simplex basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the perturbed standard-form LP \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), fix a basis index set whose matrix is \(B=A_B\). The same basis remains primal and dual feasible, hence optimal, precisely while \[B^{-1}b\ge0,\qquad c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\ge0.\] These inequalities define the basis's parameter region when \(A\) and the basis indices remain fixed. Crossing one of their boundaries can invalidate the warm basis; at a degenerate boundary, arbitrarily small perturbations may change the selected basis even when the primal optimum or objective value changes little.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reused simplex basis remains optimal exactly while its basic variables and reduced costs retain the required signs; degeneracy can make basis selection highly sensitive.
assumptions_latex: The basis indices and matrix \(A\) remain fixed.
\(B=A_B\) is nonsingular.
The LP is a minimization problem in standard form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Basis retention is equivalent to \(B^{-1}b\ge0\) and \(c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\ge0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a fixed nonsingular basis in the stated minimization standard form, primal feasibility plus nonnegative reduced costs is exactly the basis-retention condition. The condition kind fits, but no parametric or postoptimality-analysis source is supplied.

children.title: Inference Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where unstable dual information cannot support dependable search inference.

knowledge_statements.title: Inference Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique dual multipliers limit multiplier-based sensitivity inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(b)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b\}\), and let \(D^*(b)\) be the nonempty set of optimal solutions of the dual \(\max\, b^{\mathsf T}y\) subject to \(A^{\mathsf T}y=c\) and \(y\ge0\). When the value is finite in a neighborhood of \(b\), its directional derivative satisfies \[v'(b;d)=\max_{y\in D^*(b)}d^{\mathsf T}y.\] Therefore one selected multiplier \(\bar y\in D^*(b)\) supports a valid directional inference only when \(d^{\mathsf T}\bar y\) attains this maximum. If different optimal multipliers give different products, interpreting an arbitrary solver multiplier as the unique marginal value is unjustified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonunique optimal multipliers, one solver-selected dual vector need not give the correct directional marginal value; inference must account for the entire dual-optimal set.
assumptions_latex: The primal value is finite near \(b\).
\(D^*(b)\) is nonempty.
The constraint matrix and objective remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A chosen \(\bar y\in D^*(b)\) is directionally valid for \(d\) only if \(d^{\mathsf T}\bar y=\max_{y\in D^*(b)}d^{\mathsf T}y\).

children.top_down_role: Conditioning and tolerance effects compromising bound or infeasibility interpretation.

Computed primal and dual quantities are assessed using finite tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the reported residuals or objective gap are not small relative to appropriately scaled problem data, the reported bound, optimality claim, or infeasibility claim is not a reliable certificate for the exact relaxation.

A relaxation certificate is numerically unreliable whenever any required inequality \(\rho_p\le\varepsilon_p\), \(\rho_d\le\varepsilon_d\), or \(\rho_g\le\varepsilon_g\) fails, or when the claimed bound changes materially under admissible rescaling or tolerance tightening. An approximate infeasibility ray is likewise unreliable unless its normalization, sign conditions, and separating inequality exceed residual uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation certificate is unreliable when scaled residuals or gaps exceed tolerances, or when rescaling and reasonable tolerance changes materially alter the claimed bound or infeasibility conclusion.

children.title: Structure Selection-Preservation Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs governing whether network, block, integral, or sparse structure should be preserved, transformed, or delegated to a generic LP solver.

children.title: Structure-Exploiting Specialization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model regimes supporting specialized network, decomposition, or operator-based methods.

children.title: Network Specialization Regime
children.top_down_role: Models sufficiently close to pure network structure for network-specific methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Specialization Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition for choosing network-specific LP methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\) be a node-arc incidence matrix or a reduced node-arc incidence matrix: each column has one \(+1\) and one \(-1\), except that deleting at most one reference-node row per connected component may leave a column with one nonzero entry. Let \(L\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\), set \(A=\begin{bmatrix}B\\L\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and let \(m=p+r\). The LP is in the pure network regime when \(r=0\). It is in a near-network specialization regime when \(r\) is small relative to \(m\) and \(n\), and handling the side constraints in \(L\) does not dominate the network-specific operations performed on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use pure network specialization when the matrix is an incidence or reduced-incidence matrix. Near-network specialization applies when the side-constraint border is small and handling it does not dominate network-specific operations.
assumptions_latex: The LP constraint matrix can be permuted into a node-arc incidence core, possibly with bound rows and a small exceptional border.
Arc costs, capacities, and supplies are represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model lies in the network specialization regime when the exceptional border is absent or sufficiently small that network algorithms with limited side-constraint handling dominate generic sparse LP treatment.

children.title: Decomposition Specialization Regime
children.top_down_role: Models with limited coupling and tractable local blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Specialization Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-angular LP regime supporting Dantzig-Wolfe or related decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\in\mathbb{N}\). For each \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), let \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n_k}\), \(c_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n_k}\), \(X_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_k}\), and \(L_k\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n_k}\), and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^r\). Consider \(\min\{\sum_{k=1}^K c_k^Tx_k:x_k\in X_k\text{ for all }k,\ \sum_{k=1}^K L_kx_k=d\}\). The model is in the decomposition specialization regime when \(r\) is small relative to \(\sum_{k=1}^K n_k\), the blocks are uncoupled except through the linking equation, and, for the objective vectors \(q_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n_k}\) generated by the decomposition method, each oracle problem \(\min\{q_k^Tx_k:x_k\in X_k\}\) is substantially cheaper than solving the complete LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposition specialization applies when a small linking system couples otherwise independent blocks and the required optimization problems over individual blocks are substantially cheaper than the complete LP.
assumptions_latex: The number of blocks satisfies \(K\in\mathbb{N}\), and block \(k\) has variables \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n_k}\).
Each local feasible set \(X_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_k}\) admits efficient optimization or extreme-point generation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The LP is in the decomposition specialization regime when the coupling dimension is small relative to total model size and the local block subproblems remain tractable.

children.title: Generic Sparse-Solver Regime
children.top_down_role: Sparse models lacking sufficiently strong special structure for dedicated methods.

assumptions_latex: The LP matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is sparse.
No permutation exposes a sufficiently small coupling border or a dominant network-incidence structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model belongs to the generic sparse-solver regime, so exploitation should primarily use matrix sparsity, scaling, ordering, and sparse linear algebra rather than a dedicated structural algorithm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fallback regime for sparse LPs without exploitable stronger structure.

This classification is relative to a solver and hardware environment: the decisive predicate is that sparse factorization and generic presolve exploit the available structure more effectively than maintaining a specialized network or decomposition representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse LP is in this regime when neither network nor block decomposition structure is strong enough to outperform generic sparse presolve and factorization.

children.title: Dense-Linking Border-Growth Pathology

children.title: Dense Linking Rows
children.top_down_role: Globally coupled rows that weaken block separability.

assumptions_latex: Columns are partitioned into blocks of sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_K\).
A set of \(r\) constraints couples multiple column blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rows are dense linking rows when their nonzero counts grow proportionally with the aggregate sizes of the blocks they couple.

notation.meaning: support of row j within block k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic definition relative to a prescribed block partition.

source_refs.locator: 6. Large scale optimization p. 231

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of bordered block systems \(A=\begin{bmatrix}D\\L\end{bmatrix}\), let \(S_{jk}=\{i:(L_k)_{ji}\ne0\}\). A linking row \(j\) is dense on a coupled block set \(I_j\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\}\) if there exists a constant \(\alpha>0\), independent of problem size, such that \(\sum_{k\in I_j}|S_{jk}|\ge\alpha\sum_{k\in I_j}n_k\). It is globally dense linking when \(I_j\) contains all blocks. Such a row couples variables from otherwise separate local systems through one border constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linking row is dense when it touches a fixed positive fraction of the variables in the blocks that it couples.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Linking Rows

children.top_down_role: Globally coupled columns that connect otherwise sparse model components.

assumptions_latex: Rows are partitioned into local blocks of sizes \(m_1,\ldots,m_K\).
A set of variables participates in constraints from multiple row blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The columns are dense linking columns when their nonzero counts grow proportionally with the aggregate sizes of the row blocks they couple.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of matrices whose local rows are partitioned into blocks, let \(T_{kj}=\{i:C_{ij}\ne0\text{ in row block }k\}\). A linking column \(j\) is dense on a coupled block set \(I_j\) if there exists a constant \(\alpha>0\), independent of problem size, such that \(\sum_{k\in I_j}|T_{kj}|\ge\alpha\sum_{k\in I_j}m_k\). It is globally dense linking when it has this property across all row blocks. Such a column makes one variable participate broadly in otherwise separate local constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linking column is dense when it touches a fixed positive fraction of the constraints in the row blocks that it couples.

children.title: Border-Matrix Growth
children.top_down_role: Expansion of dense border structure in block-organized LP systems.

assumptions_latex: The permuted system has block-diagonal local part \(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_1,\ldots,D_K)\).
The border contains \(r\) linking rows and \(s\) linking columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Border growth destroys a small-border regime when \(r+s\) is not asymptotically small relative to local dimensions, or when border elimination forms dense matrices whose storage or factorization dominates local work.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which bordered block structure ceases to be computationally small.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the bordered matrix as \(A=\begin{bmatrix}D&C\\L&E\end{bmatrix}\). A small-border representation requires \(r+s=o(\sum_k(m_k+n_k))\) together with sparse or cheaply applicable border blocks. Border-matrix growth occurs when transformations increase \(r\), \(s\), \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)\), or \(\operatorname{nnz}(C)\) so that this condition fails. Even with small \(r+s\), growth is computationally destructive when eliminating local blocks produces a structurally dense border Schur complement whose storage is \(\Theta((r+s)^2)\) and whose direct factorization requires \(\Theta((r+s)^3)\) arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Border growth becomes destructive when linking dimensions or densities cease to be small, or when elimination creates a dense border system dominating local computation.

children.title: Separability Loss
children.top_down_role: Loss of useful decomposition structure caused by global coupling.

knowledge_statements.title: Separability Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph characterization of structural separability destroyed by linking constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_K\), and add linking equations \(\sum_{k=1}^K L_kx_k=d\). Construct an undirected graph \(G\) with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,K\}\), placing an edge \(\{k,\ell\}\) whenever one displayed linking row has a nonzero coefficient in both block \(k\) and block \(\ell\). The displayed constraint system decomposes structurally by the connected components of \(G\). A component containing more than one vertex has lost structural separability among its blocks because no partition of that component avoids a displayed linking row crossing the partition. This syntactic conclusion need not imply intrinsic nonseparability of the feasible set when linking equations are redundant or can be removed by valid algebraic transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linking rows structurally couple blocks within each connected component of the interaction graph, although redundant or algebraically removable links need not make the feasible set intrinsically nonseparable.
assumptions_latex: The number of blocks satisfies \(K\in\mathbb{N}\), and the initial feasible set is \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_K\).
Additional constraints have the form \(\sum_{k=1}^K L_kx_k=d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Structural separability in the displayed formulation is lost within every multiblock connected component of \(G\), subject to the distinction between displayed coupling and redundant or algebraically removable equations.

notation.meaning: block-interaction graph of the displayed linking rows
local feasible set for block k

children.title: Sparse-Factorization Consequences
children.top_down_role: Fill, memory, and arithmetic impacts caused by dense linking structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Factorization Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-factorization cost after eliminating sparse local blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\begin{bmatrix}D&C\\L&E\end{bmatrix}\), where \(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_1,\ldots,D_K)\) and every \(D_k\) is nonsingular. Eliminating the local variables forms the border Schur complement \(S=E-LD^{-1}C\). If \(S\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}\) is structurally dense and is treated by a conventional unstructured direct factorization, storing its factor requires \(\Theta(q^2)\) memory and factoring it requires \(\Theta(q^3)\) arithmetic. Consequently, sparse local factors alone do not ensure a low-cost overall solve: Schur-complement formation, storage, and factorization must also be included in the total cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating sparse local blocks can create a dense border Schur complement whose conventional direct factorization requires quadratic memory and cubic arithmetic, so local sparsity alone does not guarantee an inexpensive solve.
assumptions_latex: The local block matrix is \(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_1,\ldots,D_K)\), with each \(D_k\) nonsingular.
The induced border Schur complement \(S\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}\) is structurally dense and is handled by conventional unstructured direct factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Direct border storage is \(\Theta(q^2)\) and dense direct factorization is \(\Theta(q^3)\), independently of whether the local block factors remain sparse.

children.top_down_role: Lifted representations whose auxiliary structure increases coupling or memory cost.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Auxiliary-variable fill occurs when eliminating \(z\), or factoring the lifted system, creates substantially more coupling and nonzeros than the original formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(D\) is nonsingular. Eliminating auxiliary variables gives \((A-BD^{-1}C)x=b-BD^{-1}e\). Auxiliary-variable fill is present when \(BD^{-1}C\) contains nonzeros connecting original row or column blocks that were uncoupled in \(A\), or when the elimination graph of the lifted coefficient matrix produces such connections during factorization. For a fixed ordering, the fill count is the number of factor nonzeros absent from the corresponding matrix pattern. The lift is structurally harmful when this fill or the storage for \(z\) outweighs the sparsity gained by expressing the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lift causes auxiliary-variable fill when eliminating or factoring its auxiliary variables connects formerly separate blocks and increases factor storage enough to erase reformulation benefits.

children.title: Network-Integrality Contamination Boundary
children.top_down_role: Additional rows or columns that destroy pure network or total-unimodular structure.

children.title: Network-Structure Contamination
children.top_down_role: Additional model structure that disrupts a pure network representation.

assumptions_latex: The original matrix \(B\) is a node-arc incidence matrix.
Rows or columns not representable as ordinary node balances or arcs are appended.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented model is network-contaminated when the exceptional rows or columns prevent the complete matrix from being represented as a node-arc incidence matrix, even though a network core remains.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural contamination of a network matrix, not necessarily loss of total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) have in each arc column exactly one \(+1\) and one \(-1\), before optional deletion of one node row per component. An augmentation \(A=\begin{bmatrix}B&C\\R&E\end{bmatrix}\) exhibits network-structure contamination if no permitted row deletion, sign reversal, and row-column permutation makes every column of \(A\) an incidence column. This occurs, in particular, when an appended column has more than two nonzeros or incompatible coefficients, or when an appended side-constraint row makes existing arc columns violate the incidence pattern. Contamination precludes treating the entire matrix directly as a pure network matrix; it does not by itself imply loss of total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is network-contaminated when added rows or columns break the incidence-matrix pattern, although the original network core and possibly total unimodularity may remain.
knowledge_statements.title: Network-Structure Contamination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between loss of a pure incidence representation and loss of total unimodularity is important and plausible, but no source is supplied. A direct source is required for the permitted transformations and the characterization of augmented reduced-incidence matrices.

children.title: Total-Unimodularity Loss
children.top_down_role: Structural changes that remove total-unimodular matrix organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Unimodularity Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete row-addition boundary for total-unimodularity preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1\\-1&1&0\\0&-1&1\end{bmatrix}\), the node-arc incidence matrix of a directed three-cycle, and append the row \(r=(1,1,0)\). The square submatrix formed by the first two rows of \(B\) and \(r\) is \(M=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1\\-1&1&0\\1&1&0\end{bmatrix}\), and \(\det(M)=2\). Hence the augmented matrix is not totally unimodular. In general, an added row or column preserves total unimodularity exactly when every square minor newly involving that row or column belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\). If the augmented matrix is integral, failure of this condition is equivalent to the existence of a newly formed square minor whose determinant has magnitude at least \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displayed row addition creates a determinant-two minor and therefore destroys total unimodularity. Generally, preservation requires every new square minor to be minus one, zero, or one; for integral augmentations, loss is equivalent to a new minor of magnitude at least two.
assumptions_latex: A matrix is totally unimodular when every square subdeterminant belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\).
The starting matrix is a directed node-arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed augmentation is not totally unimodular because it creates a minor of determinant \(2\); the magnitude-at-least-two characterization applies generally when the augmented matrix is integral.

notation.meaning: incidence matrix of a directed three-cycle
square minor witnessing loss of total unimodularity

children.title: Row-Addition Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Added-row patterns that compromise network or integral LP structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Row-Addition Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that one added coupling row can destroy total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=(1\;1)\), which is totally unimodular, and append the row \(r=(1\;-1)\). The resulting matrix is \[\widetilde A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] Its determinant is \(\det(\widetilde A)=-2\), so \(\widetilde A\) is not totally unimodular. Thus even a row having coefficients only in \(\{-1,0,1\}\) can cross the network-integrality boundary when it couples columns with an incompatible sign pattern; coefficientwise admissibility alone does not preserve total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a single signed coupling row can create a determinant of magnitude two, destroying total unimodularity even though every new coefficient is 0, 1, or −1.
assumptions_latex: \(A=(1\;1)\) is the original constraint matrix.
\(r=(1\;-1)\) is appended as an additional row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\det(\widetilde A)\rvert=2\), hence \(\widetilde A\) is not totally unimodular.

notation.meaning: Matrix obtained after appending the new row.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The determinant calculation and failure-boundary content are mathematically correct and fit the row-addition leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source. A specific total-unimodularity theorem or counterexample locator is required.

children.title: Column-Addition Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Added-column patterns that compromise network or integral LP structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Column-Addition Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that one generated column can destroy total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}\), which is totally unimodular, and append the column \(a=(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}\). The augmented matrix is \[\widehat A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] Since \(\det(\widehat A)=-2\), the augmented matrix is not totally unimodular. Consequently, a generated column whose entries individually belong to \(\{-1,0,1\}\) need not preserve network integrality; preservation depends on its joint minor structure with the existing columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A new signed column may form a determinant of magnitude two with an existing column, so valid-looking coefficients do not by themselves preserve total unimodularity.
assumptions_latex: \(A=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}\) is the original matrix.
\(a=(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}\) is appended as a new column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\det(\widehat A)\rvert=2\), hence \(\widehat A\) is not totally unimodular.

notation.meaning: Matrix obtained after appending the new column.

children.title: Integrality Loss Consequences
children.top_down_role: Fractionality and solver impacts following structural contamination.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Loss Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral right-hand sides no longer guarantee integral vertices after total-unimodularity loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R_{+}^{2}:Bx=b\}\), where \[B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}.\] Although \(b\) is integral, the two equations uniquely determine \(x=(1/2,1/2)^{\mathsf T}\). Hence \(P\) has a fractional vertex and the linear program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\) has that fractional optimum for every \(c\in\mathbb R^{2}\). Thus loss of total unimodularity invalidates the automatic integrality guarantee, though it does not imply that every integral right-hand side produces a fractional vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After total unimodularity is lost, an integral right-hand side may yield a fractional vertex and fractional LP optimum; integrality is no longer automatic.
assumptions_latex: \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(b=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{(1/2,1/2)^{\mathsf T}\}\), so its unique vertex is fractional despite \(b\in\mathbb Z^{2}\).

notation.meaning: Feasible polyhedron of the contaminated formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed system uniquely yields the fractional point (1/2,1/2), and counterexample is the correct kind for this consequence leaf. The record nevertheless has no source for the integrality-loss claim or example, so it cannot pass evidence review.

children.title: Structure Preservation Criteria
children.top_down_role: Criteria for retaining network, block, integral, or sparse LP structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure Preservation Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ghouila-Houri criterion applied to the matrix after structural modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\{0,1,-1\}^{m\times n}\) be the matrix obtained after adding, deleting, or reorganizing rows or columns. The modification preserves total unimodularity exactly when, for every subset \(R\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), there exists a signing \(s:R\to\{-1,1\}\) such that \[\sum_{i\in R}s(i)M_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}\qquad\text{for every }j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.\] If this condition holds and \(b\) is integral, every vertex of \(\{x\in\mathbb R^{n}:Mx\le b\}\) is integral whenever a vertex exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A modification preserves total unimodularity precisely when every row subset admits signs making each signed column sum 0, 1, or −1.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in\mathbb Z^{m}\) for the stated integrality consequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The signed-row-subset predicate is equivalent to total unimodularity of \(M\); with integral \(b\), all vertices of \(\{x:Mx\le b\}\) are integral.

notation.meaning: Constraint matrix after the proposed structural modification.
Signing assigned to the selected rows.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed-row-subset condition is the Ghouila-Houri characterization, and condition is the appropriate content kind. The stated integral-vertex consequence is also standard, but neither claim has an inspectable theorem, section, or page citation.

children.title: Generic Solver Delegation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where preserved structure is secondary to a generic LP solver interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Generic Solver Delegation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal regime for delegating a contaminated structured LP to a general LP algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S\) be a structured LP class and let algorithm \(A_{\mathcal S}\) have a stated correctness or complexity guarantee only for instances in \(\mathcal S\). For a transformed instance \(I'\), if a required membership predicate fails so that \(I'\notin\mathcal S\), that guarantee cannot be invoked. If \(I'\) remains a finite linear program and a generic algorithm \(A_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is guaranteed on all such LPs, delegation to \(A_{\mathrm{LP}}\) preserves the generic correctness guarantee, although the specialized complexity bound or integrality mechanism may be lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a transformed LP fails a required structural predicate, use a general LP algorithm; correctness remains available, but specialized speed or integrality guarantees may disappear.
assumptions_latex: \(A_{\mathcal S}\) is guaranteed only on the structured class \(\mathcal S\).
\(I'\notin\mathcal S\) is nevertheless a finite linear program.
\(A_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is correct for every finite LP in its declared input model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The guarantee of \(A_{\mathcal S}\) is inapplicable to \(I'\), while the generic correctness guarantee of \(A_{\mathrm{LP}}\) applies.

notation.meaning: Structured class required by the specialized method.
